channel.title: Personal News Feed — Technology & Science
channel.description: Personally scored technology & science articles curated by news-filter

item.title: Physicist does the math on Star Trek’s “Picard maneuver”
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.62
It turns out Jean-Luc Picard was an even better starship helmsman than the writers knew. A physicist has gone through the details of a warp-speed trick from the first season of Star Trek: The Next Generation and found a subtlety the show missed. But instead of a plot hole, the detail he found actually makes the maneuver more impressive… as well as a great opportunity to teach about a lesser-known feature of the theory of relativity. Níckolas de Aguiar Alves, a physicist at the Federal University of ABC in Brazil, first watched Next Generation as a master’s student. When he got to the episode “The Battle” in the show’s first season, the plot reminded him of his relativity coursework. In “The Battle,” a Ferengi leader reminds Picard of a battle he fought years ago as captain of a ship called the Stargazer. Under fire from a mysterious attacker, Picard’s ship’s shields were down. He had to get closer without taking a hit, so he made a gamble. Picard ordered the Stargazer to charge the enemy ship at warp speed (meaning faster than light), then stop abruptly and fire. By going faster than light, Picard anticipated that the other ship would see two images of the Stargazer: where it reached warp speed and where it stopped. If they fired on the wrong image, they would miss the Stargazer, and Picard could win the battle. Later in the episode, Riker mentions that the trick had been immortalized in Starfleet textbooks as the “Picard maneuver.” As it turns out, it’s also not that far from what you can find in some physics textbooks. While warp speed is pure science fiction, physicists sometimes need to consider what happens when an object goes faster than light, and such an object really does leave two images. Something about the story bothered de Aguiar Alves at the time. But he forgot about it until years later, when he was working through a more practical problem involving particles in a medium with a slower speed of light. Not trusting that he had done the math right, he started trying to work out the situation visually.

item.title: Artemis II commander and pilot become NASA's first astronaut emeriti
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.35
The commander and pilot of NASA’s Artemis II mission have gained a new distinction five months after splashing down from the Moon: They’re not fully retiring from the space agency. Reid Wiseman and Victor Glover are the first astronauts to join NASA’s emeritus program, enabling them to continue to support the work being done at Johnson Space Center in Houston. They will remain available to train and mentor the current workforce while still being able to pursue employment and opportunities outside of NASA. “I have asked NASA … to not use the term ‘retire’ as much, but technically emeritus is a retirement program,” Glover told collectSPACE.com on Wednesday. “It’s something we have typically done for scientists when they have groundbreaking research, and they want to go back to academia to teach or to research and publish.” Glover has accepted a full-time administrative leadership position at his alma mater, California Polytechnic State University (Cal Poly) in San Luis Obispo, helping shape the school’s long-term strategies. Concurrently, he has committed to NASA to be available to convey his knowledge of the Orion spacecraft and its systems, among other expertise, to future Artemis missions. “You can be paid or you can be a gratis service, which is compensation waived, and that’s what I’m doing,” Glover said. “So I’m not going to be paid for it, but I’ll be able to voluntarily be an advisor or a consultant providing insight into what living in Orion is like.” Glover will be issued an access badge and plans to be present at the training simulation runs and hopes to be a part of establishing a new initiative, the United States Space Academy, serving NASA and the US Space Force.

item.title: Android can now securely migrate your logins between password managers
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 5.17
As longer, more complex passwords have become a necessity, remembering all those strings of numbers, letters, and special characters has become nearly impossible. Password managers can solve that problem, but what happens when you want to move to a different login organizer? Sure, you could manually type all your logins into a new app, but now Android can do that for you without the tedium. Google designed the new login transfer process to happen entirely on your phone, so you need the corresponding apps installed with your credentials synced. To start the move, you’ll have to find the import option in the app you want to use. The location of that feature will vary, but in Google Password Manager (built into Android), it’s near the top under the settings tab. The import option in Google Password Manager will plug in to the new migration system, while export still just creates an unencrypted CSV with your passwords that can be dumped into any app. It will be similar in other apps, so make sure to start the process in the app you want to use. Currently, this works in Google’s app, 1Password, Bitwarden, and Dashlane.

item.title: Panic builds over bankrupt Spirit’s looming data sale to Google
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 4.69
Doug Kreuzkamp was shocked when news outlets reported that Google won an auction to buy a huge amount of operational data as part of Spirit Airlines’ bankruptcy proceedings. Kreuzkamp founded a startup called Springshot in 2011, which created a widely used proprietary platform that helps humans and AI systems improve airline efficiency and quickly solve logistics problems so flights can stay on time and airlines can operate as smoothly as possible. Hundreds of airports use it globally. Springshot powered Spirit’s technology stack for the last three years, right up to the “very last flight,” Kreuzkamp told Ars. Yet his company got no notice when Spirit prepared to auction off a massive dataset that he thinks likely improperly includes a substantial amount of data and intellectual property (IP) that Springshot owns—not Spirit. In a limited objection filed last month, Springshot argued that Spirit’s sale agreement does not make it clear what data is being sold. It only vaguely references categories of data that would possibly rope in Springshot data, including “productivity and collaboration data,” “core business systems and business application data,” and “workflow and process data.” “This expansive definition does nothing to differentiate between Springshot’s intellectual property that exists within Spirit’s data repositories and systems, but Spirit does not own, and Spirit data that it actually owns and has the capacity to sell,” Springshot argued. Springshot urged the court to pause Spirit’s data sale until a transparent forensic process establishes that none of the data Google is grabbing is actually owned by third parties. If the bankruptcy court does not “pump the brakes,” it risks sanctioning an “unauthorized acquisition and use of trade secrets” that could doom startups, Springshot alleged. In an email to Ars, Springshot summarized its fears as the court possibly creating “a precedent where startups see massive amounts of IP transferred to the world’s richest and most monopolistic companies via bankruptcy courts.”

item.title: Europe will go it alone on Venus mission after NASA yanks radar instrument
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 4.38
The European Space Agency is moving “full steam ahead” with development of a robotic mission to Venus after NASA officials determined they were unlikely to fulfill a commitment to provide a US-built radar instrument for the spacecraft, the mission’s project scientist said. The European orbiter, named Envision, will map the Venusian surface at 10 times higher resolution than the last radar mission sent to Venus by NASA in the 1990s. The planet is enshrouded in a blanket of thick clouds of sulfuric acid, rendering its mysterious surface unseen by optical cameras in orbit. Radar is the most effective way to penetrate the clouds of Venus to reveal the terrain below, and scientists will use Envision to look for signs of active volcanism. NASA and ESA signed a memorandum of understanding in 2024 outlining their partnership on Envision. NASA agreed to supply a US-made synthetic aperture radar instrument, Envision’s primary means of mapping the surface of Venus, along with providing tracking and communications support through NASA’s Deep Space Network. In exchange, ESA would include US researchers on Envision’s science team. Europe would build the Envision spacecraft and the rest of its science instruments and provide the launch on an Ariane 6 rocket. But NASA’s budget for science missions is under the gun from the Trump administration, which proposed slashing the agency’s science funding nearly in half in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Congress rejected most of the cuts in 2026, when lawmakers passed a budget with $2.54 billion for NASA’s planetary science division, far above the White House’s request, but about $220 million shy of last year’s funding. That saved several key science missions from the chopping block, including one of NASA’s own Venus missions, called DAVINCI, designed to send an entry probe into the planet’s crushing atmosphere. But the shortfall is forcing NASA managers to make tough decisions. The primary targets for cuts in science are NASA’s funding for operating missions, especially those well beyond their original design lives, and support for partnerships on international missions.

item.title: China’s drone supremacy shows in airlifting bodies and food after Nepal flood disaster
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 3.48
Chinese-made drones are flying out the bodies of flood victims and delivering food to survivors in the aftermath of devastating flash floods on the border of Nepal and China’s Tibetan region. Nepal’s army has been using four DJI FlyCart 100 drones donated from China to make 10 to 16 aid deliveries each day, according to Reuters. This comes after a partial glacier collapse in the Himalayan mountains unleashed a sudden surge of water, mud, and debris that swept through border crossings, valley communities, and hydropower projects on August 26. The DJI Flycart 100 Drones come with a 98-foot rope and winch system for picking up and dropping off heavy loads. The website of Chinese drone company DJI describes the drones as being able to carry between 187 and 220 pounds, depending on the battery configuration. The four Chinese cargo drones being used by the Nepal army are currently hauling about 132 pounds of supplies per trip, Reuters reported. That heavy-lift capability has also allowed the drones to remove human bodies from some flood-stricken areas. The official death toll in Nepal had risen to 1,369 as of September 9, according to a situation report from the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. The Nepal government agency also reported that more than 5,000 people are still missing, including 587 foreign nationals. The same situation report also mentioned how the drones have helped to distribute 1,591 kilograms of food items across 31 flights. The United Nations is appealing for $20.5 million to help 43,000 people in the aftermath of the flood disaster in Nepal. Smaller drones have also proven useful in search-and-rescue efforts as Nepal has deployed more than 21,000 police and soldiers to look for survivors. Search teams have occasionally found surviving workers trapped in hydropower tunnels after the floodwaters ripped through both operational hydropower plants and sites under construction.

item.title: Boy developed "toasted skin" condition from using a laptop every day
item.description:
Source: Ars Technica Score: 3.33
Fears that modern electronic devices may harm children are nothing new. Gadgets with screens of any size have long been allegedly melting, rotting, and/or corrupting the brains of youths for decades. However, a medical case report published this week offers a new and alarming way our digital doodads may cause physical harm. In BMJ Case Reports, two UK doctors, Mara Znagoveanu and Edward Artley, report the case of a boy who came to an emergency department with alarming marks on his abdomen. The marks were described as being in a patch about 15 centimeters (six inches) wide, made of flat, reddish-brown “interlacing lines forming irregular circles and a lace-like morphology.” A picture of the marks is here. Mysterious marks The boy, whom they described only as being in “mid-childhood,” was not in any pain, and the rash was not warm to the touch or tender. He and his parents said they couldn’t think of any recent injuries or trauma that might explain the marks. He was otherwise healthy, hadn’t recently been ill, and had no systemic symptoms, such as fever or fatigue. Everything about the boy’s health, growth, and medical history looked normal. Nurses in the emergency department initially described it as “spontaneous bruising.” A physical exam yielded no insights; there were no other skin abnormalities, abdominal tenderness, or signs of organ trouble. They did a chest X-ray, searching for an explanation. It revealed a small patch of whiteness over his left lung, indicating cells or fluid, such as pus or blood. As the doctors were taking blood for further testing, the boy told them that he did have one injury: About a week prior, around when the marks appeared, he was play-fighting with his siblings and got pushed into a chair. He said he didn’t mention it before because he didn’t want his siblings to get in trouble. The new information pointed the doctors to the idea of an underlying traumatic injury. They did a computed tomography (CT) scan, looking for internal abdominal injuries. But they found none, besides the small blip in his lungs that the X-ray showed—which could have just been incidental from a minor infection.

item.title: NASA and IBM made an AI model for exploring the Moon
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.90
NASA and IBM made an AI model for exploring the Moon The two organizations are also releasing a dataset researchers can use to make their own models. This past spring, the world experienced a rare moment of collective joy and awe when NASA's Artemis II mission, the first crewed flight to the Moon since 1972, completed its historic lunar flyby. On April 6, astronauts Reid Wiseman, Christina Koch, Victor Glover and Jeremy Hansen flew farther from Earth than any humans before them. Now, as NASA prepares for the next Artemis mission and beyond, the space agency is working with IBM to give scientists new tools to study the Moon. On Thursday, the two organizations released the NASA-IBM Lunar Foundation Model. It's an open-source AI system that's available to download from Hugging Face. As a foundation model, it can do a few different things, says Dr. Juan Bernabé-Moreno, the director of IBM Research Europe, UK and Ireland. To start, NASA and IBM found it was particularly adept at identifying areas on the lunar surface where there might be ice. The two organizations ran a test where they compared the model's predictions against a map they made using a published scientific workflow that incorporates terrain, thermal and other environmental data. They then pitted the model against SwinV2-B, a Microsoft-trained vision system for processing high-resolution images. The NASA-IBM model reduced errors by 23 percent. NASA and IBM compared the model against SwinV2-B because the tool is often used as the baseline for many image analysis tasks. NASA and IBM also benchmarked their model's ability to identify and classify craters. There, the new model outperformed SwinV2-B by 19 percent while using half the training data. NASA and IBM got a chance to verify the model's capabilities recently when a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket crashed into the Moon on August 5. When IBM fed an image of the impact to the model, it correctly identified the crash site as a new crater, despite it closely overlapping with an existing crater. "It worked fantastically," says Bernabé-Moreno, with the model nailing the identification on its first attempt. Bernabé-Moreno says training the model was a challenge. "In Earth observation, you have pristine images," he explains. Our planet's atmosphere scatters sunlight, filling shadows with ambient light that softens their edges. Shadows on the Moon instead appear knife-edged and pitch black, meaning any time they're photographed, the shadowed pixels don't carry any information. "On the Moon, what you have is the sun at different moments during the day, and it illuminates and it cuts shadows, and you need to deal with those shadows," he says. The result is that a crater can look one way in one image and completely different in the next image. Another challenge came as a result of how computer vision models are typically trained and tested. Most often, that process involves removing some parts of an image and then tasking the model with reconstructing what's missing based on the patterns it has learned in training. "You might remove 90 percent of a crater, and with [the remaining] 10 percent, you ask the model to reconstruct the other 90 percent," explains Bernabé-Moreno. That doesn't work for the Moon. As you might imagine, the reason for that is that a lot of craters look very similar to one another when photographed from orbit. In fact, IBM's attempts to train the model in the traditional way were a "complete disaster," says Bernabé-Moreno, but the research team eventually devised a creative solution. "We took the Moon and divided it into wedges, like an orange, and we completely separated the training wedges from the testing wedges. This way, we could give the model a lot of consistency," he says. One of the reasons NASA and IBM are excited about this release is that it includes a first-of-its-kind open-source dataset that other researchers can use to build future models. It incorporates tens of thousands of images and instrument data from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Gravity Recovery and Interior Laboratory (GRAIL) missions, as well as Japan's Selenological and Engineering Explorer (SELENE). "One of the reasons we've never seen a comprehensive, powerful lunar model before is that we didn't have the data [organized] in the right way," says Bernabé-Moreno. Organization in this case meant creating a grid where every pixel of imaging data corresponds to other modalities of data a model can use to inform its processing. "That alone is a massive scientific contribution, because put the model aside: the community now has a co-registered dataset with more than two million [data] points," says Bernabé-Moreno. "And we know that AI models get superseded by other models. The data is what really creates the industry of AI models."

item.title: Universal Music Group is collaborating with ElevenLabs on a new AI-powered creation platform
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.48
Universal Music Group is collaborating with ElevenLabs on a new AI-powered creation platform The unnamed software will be built around licensed music from UMG artists who want to participate. Universal Music Group and ElevenLabs have announced a new multi-year licensing agreement and "wider strategic collaboration" that will see them launch a new AI-powered licensed music platform. The deal with UMG is the first that ElevenLabs has cut with a major label, and the new platform will be distinct from its ElevenMusic AI music generation software. The two companies also intend to collaborate on new AI audio products that can be used by artists, UMG wrote in a press release. The AI creation software, which seemingly doesn't yet have a name, is still in development, and no release date is mentioned. It will primarily be aimed at music fans who want to make remixes and mashups of music from participating and "fairly compensated" artists that are signed to the label. ElevenLabs' tools will also be able to create "new track interpretations and personalized vocal experiences." The music industry has had a complicated relationship with the emergence of AI. Just a few months ago a coalition of major labels that included UMG issued a collective appeal for AI slop tracks to be banned from charts worldwide, while various legal battles between labels and AI companies like Suno and Udio over accusations of copyright infringement have been well documented in the last few years. A number of these lawsuits, though, such as one filed by Warner against Udio in 2024, have ultimately ended in settlements and licensing deals being struck. And just this week, Suno said that the launch of its new v6 AI music models marked the formal beginning of its relationships with labels like Warner and BMG.

item.title: iOS 27 brings GymKit to iPhone and AirPods, but what does it actually do?
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.36
iOS 27 brings GymKit to iPhone and AirPods, but what does it actually do? GymKit never became as popular as it should have, but great compatibility could fix that. Released in October 2017, Apple's GymKit is an exciting idea that was never widely adopted. The premise is simple: you tap your watch to a machine in the gym to enable data syncing in both directions. The gym equipment can display what your watch is measuring, while your watch uses the machine's metrics to better calculate the quality of your workout. However, gym equipment replacement tends to be a slow process and purchasing equipment for the home is getting more expensive every year. Given the need for an Apple Watch and a compatible cardio machine, Apple's exercise API has had a lot working against it. With iOS 27, however, Apple is bringing GymKit to iPhone. With this update, your AirPods Pro 3 will handle heart rate data, while the iPhone becomes the screen and record-keeper for workouts. The exercise machine completes the trifecta, contributing its own gathered workout information to the Fitness app. Nothing has changed on the compatibility front. The cardio machine still needs Apple's GymKit integration, whether you're using an Apple Watch or an iPhone. iOS 27 just adds the same tap-to-connect option for iPhone, so you use the NFC reader with your phone instead of your watch. Without GymKit integration, iPhones and AirPods are still useful for ordinary workout tracking. They just won't pull any data from the exercise equipment. How iPhone and AirPods fit into GymKit With iOS 27, the process of connecting with GymKit is the same as using your iPhone to pay at a store. With a compatible machine handy, tap the iPhone on the GymKit or NFC connection point, choose the type of workout and start the session. Treadmills, ellipticals, bikes and stair steppers are mentioned among the supported types of cardio equipment, but compatibility may extend to other units as well. If you're wearing AirPods Pro 3, the earbuds will provide live heart rate data to your iPhone, which feeds that information to the equipment, which sends workout details to the Fitness app. It's all one big, clean circle of data. According to Apple's GymKit privacy page, the workout information is removed from the connected equipment once your workout session ends, unless you're using a machine you've signed into. The point is that you no longer need an Apple Watch to take advantage of workout features that were once exclusive to the wearable. If you forget to charge your watch, you can still connect to compatible workout equipment with an iPhone and AirPods Pro 3. What GymKit does and doesn't replace Unfortunately, this new functionality is not a full-fledged replacement of the Apple Watch. Your iPhone and compatible AirPods supply all the data you could realistically need from a workout session. But the Apple Watch is a broader tool that provides the all-day, all-night data context to go along with daily workout routines. There are practical limitations, too. You must have your iPhone updated to iOS 27, and need AirPods Pro 3 for heart rate tracking. As of this writing, GymKit-supported cardio machines will disconnect from an iPhone if AirPods Pro 3 aren't also in the mix. Perhaps the biggest obstacle is compatible workout equipment, since many of the machines common in gyms and home setups don't work with GymKit. If you don't own an Apple Watch, tend to forget it at home or don't charge it on a regular basis, the iOS 27 update paired with AirPods Pro 3 will do the trick in a pinch. Due to the practical constraints of needing your phone and AirPods, though, wearing a charged and ready-to-go Apple Watch is still the more convenient option.

item.title: IDScan is offering free credit monitoring and ID protection after leaking driver's licenses
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.16
IDScan is offering free credit monitoring and ID protection after leaking driver's licenses The platform was linked to an FBI investigation into a dark web marketplace last week. IDScan.net, an ID fraud protection platform, has announced it's offering "free credit monitoring and identity protection services" as a make good for customers impacted by a recent data security incident. The company hasn't publicly connected this breach to a report last week that its data was a possible source for a new dark web marketplace selling scans of IDs online. The timing of this announcement certainly raises the possibility, though. "While the investigation is ongoing, IDScan.net has determined that an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud," the company said. "The type of information contained within the affected data may have included full names and driver's license or other government-issued identification numbers." According to IDScan.net, full access to the information "required payment," but it's still contacting people potentially impacted by the incident and providing free credit monitoring and identity protection services. The company also says it's "cooperating with federal law enforcement on their investigation." Writing for his blog KrebsonSecurity on September 1, journalist Brian Krebs reported that Nexus, a dark web ID marketplace, was selling scans of over 153 million US and Canadian driver's licenses and millions of other ID documents. Nexus reportedly shuttered ahead of an FBI investigation into the marketplace, but Krebs' report cited IDScan as a possible source for the ID documents it was selling. Engadget has asked IDScan.net to comment on the report and the possible connection between its security incident and Nexus. We'll update this article if we hear back.

item.title: Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 5.11
Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids They both include a giant green button to access a child's favorite content. Yoto just announced two new audio devices for kids. There's the fourth-generation Yoto Player and an updated version of the Yoto Mini. The new Yoto Player is still a speaker with a pixel display, but the company has added some bells and whistles. Firstly, there's a big green dial that kids can twist to play their "most loved audio." This can access up to 20 pieces of content, including podcasts, stories and songs. This is done directly from the device, so there will be no need for a kid to borrow a parent's phone. Additionally, the functionality doesn't require Yoto Cards, which are basically little NFC keys that get inserted into the player to access unique content. The company has also upgraded the software so routines are easier to create and access. This means that parents can set up a routine just one time and the device will automatically do stuff like adjust the graphics to reflect the time of day. Yoto promises that the hardware has been redesigned so it's "easy for little hands." The storage has been increased up to 64GB, downloads should be much faster and the nightlight panel has been upgraded. All of this is very good news, considering an older version of the Yoto Player already made our list of the best audio gadgets for kids. However, there is a spot of bad news. The price is shooting up to $150, from $110. It's available to pre-order right now, with shipments going out on October 15. The Yoto Mini is also getting a nice little hardware refresh. This is the company's cheaper and much smaller audio player. The upcoming Mini looks to be designed for the kind of adventures kids typically get into. It's "rugged, water and dust-resistant." The company promises it can "handle playground grass, sofa launches and rainy-day chaos without missing a beat." The upgrade also includes the same green button that allows access to content without Yoto Cards. The device has enough storage for "1,000 hours of audio" and it integrates with both wired and Bluetooth headphones. Sadly, there's another price increase here. The Yoto Mini is going up to $110, from $80. It's available for pre-order right now, with shipments going out on September 30. The company is also introducing several accessories for its devices. There are scratch-proof cases for both the Mini and Player that are available in four colors. It's also working on a wireless dock and a case for Yoto Cards. We don't have pricing or availability information on this stuff just yet.

item.title: Anthropic caught scientists using Claude to further biological weapon research
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 4.49
Anthropic caught scientists using Claude to further biological weapon research The company has produced an extensive collection of case studies covering the ways its current AI models have been misused. Anthropic has flagged and stopped multiple scientists who were using its AI models to create potential biological weapons, according to a new report the company shared on Thursday. "Biological misuse" is just one flavor of troubling AI usage the report documents, but it's of growing importance because newer models like Fable 5 are increasingly good at helping with scientific research. The company's report includes five case studies of Anthropic's models being used to develop biological weapons, the safety measures that brought the misuse to Anthropic's attention and how it responded. Detecting possible misuse is complicated, as the company stressed to The New York Times, because research into a new vaccine could look a lot like creating a bioweapon. In all cases the company says it erred on the side of being overly cautious because of the possible consequences. "You are not seeing someone in a comic book kind of way say, 'Hey, I want to build a biological weapon to kill everybody,'" Jacob Klein, Anthropic's head of threat intelligence, told The New York Times. "It's an incredibly nuanced situation." In one case study from May, Anthropic says its "biological safety classifier" flagged a request for Claude to author a grant for gain-of-function research on chikungunya virus. The virus has no licensed treatment and can cause debilitating symptoms for weeks or months, the company says. Gain-of-function research explores methods for genetically altering an organism, and in the case of this specific virus, the grant proposed increasing its transmissibility and ability to evade immune response. The combination sounds dangerous, and Anthropic says the fact that the proposed research was affiliated with a military research institute made it extra questionable. The company took similar issue with gain-of-function research into bird flu and a separate case of a researcher using Claude to develop an atlas of venom toxin peptides and "a generative pipeline that optimized toxin characteristics." The full report also includes case studies on Anthropic's models being used as a surveillance tool and to create software exploits, propaganda and weapons systems. According to the company, anyone misusing Claude or Anthropic models had their account banned, and the findings from the investigation are being used to further improve model safeguards and prevent future misuse. Given the tricky nature of biological misuse, Anthropic is also not naming the individuals or institutions its investigation connected to the development of possible biological weapons. "The individuals implicated in these case studies are working scientists," Anthropic says. "We do not assert that they intended harm, and identifying them or their labs could expose them to harm."

item.title: A native Gemini app is finally available for Windows PCs
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 3.90
A native Gemini app is finally available for Windows PCs There's a keyboard shortcut to open it up, just like the Mac version. Google has finally released a native Gemini app for Windows 10 and 11. This provides a streamlined way to use the AI tools on Windows PCs and follows a Mac release earlier this year. Once downloaded, users can pull up the Gemini app via a keyboard shortcut, just like how it works on Mac computers. The company says this is great when people "need a quick fact-check on a document or a few catchy title ideas for a presentation." I would recommend fact-checking that fact-check because, you know, it's generative AI. The @GeminiApp is now available for Windows Just press Alt + Space to bring instant Gemini assistance right to your desktop alongside your favorite apps and tools. pic.twitter.com/g3wbdvzxii — Google (@Google) September 10, 2026 The app integrates with other Google AI products, so tasks can be sent to the agentic assistant Gemini Spark. It even works with stuff like Gmail and Google Drive. It can also generate images and videos via Nano Banana and Gemini Omni, if that's your bag. Google promises the app is "lightweight and quiet," so it won't slow down Windows PCs. It's available for download right now and the company says more native desktop capabilities are coming down the pike in the future.

item.title: The iPhone Duo just might live up to the hype
item.description:
Source: Engadget Score: 2.93
The iPhone Duo just might live up to the hype It's got that Apple touch. Apple's foldable iPhone has arrived, finally, after almost 10 years of rumors. Given how late the company was to the foldable party, many were expecting a miss or at least something that failed to excite. I think the iPhone Duo is hitting (mostly) all the right notes. With foldables, the idea since the start was a tablet-sized screen that fits in your pocket. The best tablets are iPads, which is why the iPhone Duo matters — and not just for Apple. For the first time, the company that makes the best tablet is making a foldable. At least with iOS 27, it's still mostly an iPhone experience, not an iPad one. Many of the features are the kind that we already expect from a foldable: app multitasking, more interface elements on the 7.6-inch inner screen and multi-camera FaceTime calls. The Duo also works with the Apple Pencil, a first for the iPhone. But then there's that Apple touch: it does the obvious thing, and you wonder why no one else thought of it. With the iPhone Duo, Apple shifted the app dock to the side of the screen when it opens and did the same for menus. While the Galaxy Fold series has a similar feature, the Edge Panel is hidden away most of the time, housing tools and shortcuts like Now Brief and AI Select — things I use far less than core apps like Gmail or Messages. Like Samsung's Galaxy Z Fold 8, the iPhone Duo's screens have a more unified aspect ratio — if not precisely identical, as the company claimed in the announcement. And while it doesn't magically solve interface design complexities and wrinkles, early hands-on videos and what Apple has shown so far suggest it all looks like the UI "fits" better: it looks tidier, with more visual continuity. I like how unfolding the iPhone Duo transplants the front display screen onto the right side of the foldable display, plus the glossy transition animation that brings the other screen into focus as you unfurl. Other Apple touches are present throughout the hardware. The iPhone Duo's volume buttons are on the upper edge, so they're always in the same place regardless of which screen you use on the iPhone Duo. On the screens themselves, a nano-coating gives a matte finish that not only reduces reflections in harsh light but also helps obscure that foldable crease that companies and some die-hard phone fans are obsessed with. Why is Apple the first to do this? I think the asymmetric front-screen design is charming, too. With two curved and two squared-off corners, it's like a notepad or a book and looks cute either way. Did Apple sneak in a return to skeuomorphism? (Xiaomi beat Apple to the punch by a day, but its 18 Fold smartphone isn't launching globally.) Perhaps the biggest surprise was that, despite the typical "Apple premium" and spiraling component prices, the company's first foldable will land at $2,000. I suspected it would be several hundred dollars more. This price puts it between foldable rivals like the Pixel 11 Pro Fold ($1,899) and the Galaxy Fold 8 Ultra ($2,100), and is $100 more than the launch price of the Galaxy Fold 8's launch price. That's not the Apple I'm used to. (History note: Samsung's debut Galaxy Fold cost $1,980 in 2019.) A lot of my favorite parts of the iPhone Duo are small things that add up to a better overall experience. But aside from the matte nano-coating and Apple Pencil support, there's nothing as substantial as, say, when the company ditched the home button on the iPhone X and introduced Face ID. (Funnily enough, the iPhone Duo reverts to Touch ID.) Existing foldables already do some things better, too. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 can open and run up to five apps total: three split-screen and two in floating windows. While the iPhone Duo's two-app function may seem underwhelming, it's likely a deliberate choice by Apple, not a technical limitation. I've never used more than three apps across the 10-plus foldables I've tested and reviewed over the years, because it gets messy. Also, you can just swipe to the other apps, chill. Like Samsung's Fold 8, this is still an expensive smartphone. $2,000 is a lot for an iPhone, especially one without a telephoto camera and without the iPhone 18 Pro's headline variable-aperture camera. It's an odd look when the priciest iPhone ever lacks its best camera ever. Despite these downsides, I'm most excited by how Apple is tackling the problems (and potential) of the foldable. Conventional knowledge (and experience) suggests holding back on a first-of-its-kind device from Apple, but this isn't its first smartphone. For those aching for a foldable that wasn't running Android, it's here, and it looks like it will deliver.

item.title: AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: ANC Isn’t the Only Upgrade
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 5.64
Apple’s annual hardware event had a lot to offer this year. Easily the biggest splash came from the iPhone Duo, Apple’s first-ever foldable phone, with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max also giving its $2,000 foldable a run for its money. While a new generation of AirPods, the AirPods 5, might not achieve the same highs as a first-of-its-category iPhone, there are quite a few things you should know if you’re in the market for new AirPods without the “Pro” name. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: ANC Non-Pro AirPods aren’t known for their prowess in active noise cancellation (ANC). It’s not that Apple doesn’t have the chops; it’s that they’re only semi-in-ear, meaning they don’t have silicone ear tips. Because of that, they don’t have the same tight seal as the AirPods Pro, which helps block out sound. That being said, they do have ANC, and it’s not all created equal among generations. According to Apple, the AirPods 5 have 50% better noise cancelling than the AirPods 4, which is a pretty drastic increase. It’s hard to really relay how that feels without hearing them myself, but on paper, it’s hard to argue. If you want better ANC, the AirPods 5 are the way to go, even if AirPods Pro 3 blow both of those pairs out of the water. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Sound Good ANC doesn’t mean much if the sound isn’t just as good, and in this generation, Apple improved in that department, too. Apple says the AirPods 5 have a new “multiport architecture” that’s based on the AirPods 3 Pro. The result, according to Apple, is “richer, more detailed sound across an even wider range of ear geometries.” Sound, again, is one of those things you have to hear to believe, but clearly Apple paid attention to improving the sound quality in this generation, so you should expect a step up over the last generation. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Battery life Battery life is where things get a little more complicated. While the base model of AirPods 5 has the same battery life as its predecessor—a pretty pedestrian four hours on a single charge when ANC is activated—you can actually shell out a bit more money for a different tier with some extra juice. The $149 AirPods 5 (that’s $20 more than the base) will get you an extra hour of battery life with ANC on. That’s still not great in the scheme of most wireless earbuds (about six hours is pretty standard), but if you’re strictly comparing between generations of non-Pro AirPods, then the more expensive model of AirPods 5 definitely take the cake. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Features While both generations share a lot of the same features, there are some subtle differences to note outside of ANC. In addition to better ANC, the AirPods 5 also have next-gen Adaptive EQ, according to Apple. Thanks to this upgraded Adaptive EQ, the AirPods 5 can tune sound to the specific shape of your ears across a larger range of frequencies. The result, Apple says, is a “more immersive and accurate sound.” AirPods 4 do have Adaptive EQ, for the record, but Apple claims that the new generation just does it better. The differences continue to pile up when you consider the more expensive tier of AirPods 5. By shelling out $149, you get two things that neither the base tier of AirPods 5 nor the AirPods 4 have: wireless charging and stem controls. For the first time, the more expensive tier now lets you swipe on the wireless earbuds to control volume. Not groundbreaking, but it can be better than reaching for your phone every time. Similarly, wireless charging in the charging case isn’t mind-blowing, but it’s nice to have. AirPods 5 vs. AirPods 4: Fit This is one area where not much has changed. In its announcement, Apple didn’t say much about any kind of physical redesign, so the AirPods 5 likely look and feel pretty similar to the AirPods 4. These are still semi-open-ear, meaning they nest in your outer ear instead of being inserted like AirPods Pro.

item.title: Report: Roughly Half the World’s Governments Underestimated Covid Deaths by the Millions
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.80
Aside from maybe a few blinkered members from some of society’s more fortunate demographics (e.g., white-collar remote workers, monied introverts, etc.), most people don’t particularly recall the covid-19 pandemic fondly. But new research from social scientists in London and Jerusalem is now providing strong indications that the scope of this tragedy was far worse than many governments let on. Moses Shayo and Ariel Karlinsky, two researchers who specialize in political and health economics, compiled an unusually comprehensive dataset from “all-cause mortality” reports, taken across 134 countries and territories both before and during the covid-19 pandemic. They then compared this more concrete data, some of it obtained by local journalists via freedom of information laws, to contemporaneous official government pronouncements during the heights of the pandemic in 2020 and 2021. As many as 45% to 55% of these nations, Shayo and Karlinsky found, misreported covid’s death toll—in most cases underplaying the severity of the crisis. Compared to the 5.08 million deaths attributed to covid-19 by state officials during this two-year period, the researchers determined that the actual number of covid-related deaths (based on these governments’ own hard numbers) was more than twice that: about 12.47 million. “Our evidence shows that manipulation was remarkably widespread and large in magnitude,” Shayo and Karlinsky said in a press statement. In the 62 countries where they found covid deaths were underreported, aspiring and successful “informational autocrats” managed to avoid counting 14.5% of the expected covid deaths on average, they found. Means, motive, and opportunity Shayo and Karlinsky devoted considerable effort in their study, published in the Journal of Economic Growth, to dissecting and delineating between possible explanations for why a given country might have underreported its covid-19 deaths. Plenty of nations, they noted, simply did not have the resources to adequately keep up with the punishing deluge of deaths, whether in terms of medical diagnostics, hospital access, or sheer personnel. But, as they adjusted for these factors, the researchers found a troubling correlation indicative of multiple premeditated efforts to minimize the scope of the pandemic’s impact. Shayo and Karlinsky used state-level data on the share of adults with either a college education and/or internet access, alongside information collected by the United Nations’ Human Development Education Index, to craft a metric for each nation’s relative “audience sophistication.” The measure—when viewed alongside the structural checks and balances reining in each government’s executive power—tended to mirror the scale of underreported covid deaths. “In countries where formal and informal checks and balances are weak, executives tend to act as ‘informational autocrats,’” Shayo and Karlinsky said. “The most important set of constraints appear to be institutional constraints on the executive. Additionally, the severity of underreporting drops significantly the more sophisticated the domestic audience is,” the pair wrote in their study. “We find less evidence relating it to cultural factors and to macroeconomic incentives to underreport.” A tyranny of small decisions Shayo and Karlinsky stopped short of claiming causality, however, merely framing it as “probably noteworthy” that states with the most accurate covid-19 reporting were “strongly associated with constraints on the government’s ability to effectively manipulate information.” More benign institutional policies might lead certain state bureaucracies to repeatedly err on ambiguous deaths, leading edge cases to either be always or never logged as covid-related, they noted. “[Some] countries may be reluctant to report a given death as Covid unless they are absolutely certain the death was due to Covid, even though this violates [U.N. World Health Organization] WHO guidelines, [independent] of capacity or intention to obfuscate,” according to the pair, who are currently based at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem in Israel. (Shayo is also a professor at King’s College London). In perhaps the duo’s most unsurprising finding, Shayo and Karlinsky uncovered signs that incumbent politicians somehow succumbed to the temptation to skew government data in their favor: “There is also evidence that misreporting is higher in countries holding elections during the pandemic,” they wrote.

item.title: Apple’s Biggest AI Advantage: It’s Not Trying to Build God
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.49
Apple had a lot to talk about during its “Surprise and Shine” product launch event on Wednesday: a new CEO, revamped AirPods, an Apple Watch that can record your conversations, and of course, a much-anticipated foldable iPhone. The only thing missing was grandiose proclamations about how AI is going to revolutionize everything in the world, and maybe even kill us all. Not so long ago, believing such a thing would’ve been considered at the very least fringe, even within the sci-fi-indoctrinated ranks of Silicon Valley. It wasn’t until the arrival of ChatGPT in late 2022 that people started accepting the idea that AI—long an intellectual taboo in tech circles—could in fact become a mainstream tool, and perhaps have as big a cultural impact as the iPhone or the internet. And while people have been warning about the danger of runaway AI for decades, those fears escalated sharply earlier this year, following a series of autonomous hacks which showed how frail our existing cybersecurity infrastructure can be in the face of swarms of self-coordinating agents that tech companies seem unable (or unwilling) to control. Anxiety about the future reached a new height this week after an AI safety researcher at Anthropic named Evan Hubinger wrote in a social media post that the very technology his company is racing to build has a greater than ten percent chance of wiping out humanity. It got the world’s attention. In a sign that AGI fears had breached the mainstream, Sheryl Crow, of all people, wrote on Instagram that she was “begging and pleading that we wake up to this moment and demand our leaders put aside their greed and prevent [unconstrained AI development] from going forward.” U.S. lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle called on Congress this week to rein in the race to build artificial “superintelligence”—a term that started as a warning but has since, in a strange trick of rhetorical alchemy, been embraced as a marketing buzzword by the biggest American AI labs. Hubinger’s views on the apocalyptic potential of AI can seem confounding: Why would he help to build something he thinks could exterminate every one of us? But that idea is hardly unusual in his industry. Many of the most powerful players in the AI race have long said, quite plainly and in public, that the technology could go terribly wrong and be the agent of our extinction, whether that’d be through some engineered doomsday virus, a cybersecurity takeover, an AI-triggered nuclear exchange, or some other machine-made catastrophe our mortal minds can’t even hope to fathom. (The whole idea behind superintelligence, after all, is that it’ll be playing hyperdimensional chess while we humans are still struggling to play checkers.) Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s cofounder and CEO, has said there’s as high as a 25% chance that AI goes “really, really badly.” (Read: that humanity is toast.) Elon Musk believes there’s about a 10%-20% chance that things could go terribly wrong. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has been reluctant to assign a specific probability to that outcome, but he doesn’t believe it’s zero. In a perverse but very real way, the world-killing power of superintelligent AI is, for tech leaders, a feature, not a bug. You can’t have an all-powerful machine God capable of curing cancer and freeing us from drudgework without some risk that it’ll turn on us. That will seem deeply inhuman to most sane people who don’t have any prospect of becoming uber-wealthy from the AI boom. But make no mistake, it is a fundamental presupposition these companies are operating from, and they don’t even try to keep it a secret. The language they use is typically more dialed-down, but the bottom line, they’ll say, is that humanity should accept some chance of annihilation for a shot at the golden age they believe AI can lead us into. All of which makes Apple’s rather muted approach to AI stand out. The company has been widely regarded as a slowpoke since the debut of ChatGPT, focusing on its hardware business while just about every other tech giant did an about-face to make AI a top priority. Its launch of “Apple Intelligence” in 2024 was more of a whimper than a bang, and to this day its AI muscle is largely dependent upon models from Google, its erstwhile competitor. AI wasn’t completely absent from its Wednesday product launch event, but it was more of a background theme than the shiny center of attention. No doubt freshly minted Apple CEO John Ternus has been keeping a watchful eye on the public backlash to AI data centers and fears over an AI-pocalypse, and thinking that perhaps the best way to win over people’s hearts and minds is not to talk about AI as if it were some omnipotent God we’re summoning into being, but just another tool to help you do the things you already do, like touching up photos and getting walking directions from Siri. And for millions of people who are increasingly fearful of the future, that’s likely to be a sales pitch they can actually get behind. READ MORE:

item.title: Live Updates From Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ iPhone Event 🔴
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 3.14
A new era at Apple is upon us. Newly appointed CEO John Ternus is now at the helm of the $4.75 trillion-dollar company, and the first foldable iPhone is reportedly going to be announced this Wednesday, Sept. 9, at the company’s “Surprise and Shine” event at Apple Park. While the foldable iPhone will likely steal the show, we’re also expecting to see the rumored iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Raymond Wong, Gizmodo’s Senior Editor of Consumer Tech, and Adriano Contreras, Gizmodo’s Social Media Editor, will be reporting live from the Steve Jobs Theater before, during, and after the keynote, which kicks off at 1 p.m. ET / 10 a.m. PT. In an internal memo sent to staff on his first day as CEO, Ternus said the launch “is going to be phenomenal.” Let’s see if Apple can change the world again. Be sure to bookmark this page and check back often as we live blog it all. Don’t get too upset by any headlines you read that say the new Apple Watch Series 12 screen is smaller than previous models. However, MacRumors pointed out that the Series 12 specs page lists the screen surface area as 1,196 sq mm. The Apple Watch Series 11 watch face was 1,220 sq mm on the 46mm version. The 42mm version has dropped from 989 sq mm to 970 sq mm. That’s about a 2% difference for both versions of the Series 12. The casing is now also slightly larger, resulting in an almost imperceptible growth in the screen borders. I don’t imagine most users would be able to spot the difference, though I may be more intrigued to see screen size shrinking instead of growing, for a change. —Kyle Barr the Apple tiktok team is once again killing it (last one is insane tho 😭) pic.twitter.com/HFAGJnzWiG — Dylan (@DylanMcD8) September 10, 2026 Apple’s new Instagram and TikTok scrolling promos for the iPhone Duo are tongue-in-cheek in the way I find surprising for the Cupertino tech giant. One of the ads shows somebody at a coffee shop with their laptop and a large cup of joe, while somebody with a Duo sits next to them and receives a proportional, Alice in Wonderland-sized coffee. Another ad shows an iPhone having a nice dinner date with an iPad mini. As one of the shrinking number of tiny tablet fans, I feel almost like the crochety father who does not want my precious child mingling with the likes of iPhone. —Kyle Barr If you were wondering what the difference is between this generation of AirPods and the last generation, I got you. Spoiler alert: AirPods 5 are improved in pretty much every way. —James Pero The iPhone 18 Pro is a very similar phone to the iPhone 17 Pro, from the screen to the shape and everything in between. However, the biggest differences are more than skin deep, with some promising improvements to the iPhone’s cooling and chip design. It’s also the first iPhone with a mechanical aperture, something that will only get a few people excited. Luckily for Apple, I’m one of those people. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch Ultra and their new audio recording features have people talking, and let’s just say people keep bringing up always-recording smart glasses in the same sentence. Siri Recap is supposed to listen to you throughout the day and offer a summary of what you did and who you talked to. Live Rewind is a user-activated feature that can summarize conversations you just had. Apple’s support document detailing Siri Recap and Live Rewind mentions that they’re exclusive to the S11 processor inside the new watches. That’s partly because they have a “secure exclave” that processes this audio on-device. The document reads, “Data that is processed and analyzed in the Secure Exclave cannot be accessed by watchOS, apps, the user, or Apple.” The data in the exclave is not stored or transcribed, but the encrypted file is processed for transcription on your iPhone’s own secure exclave. Users can choose to save these summaries on their iCloud accounts. You can read the full explanation for yourself here. Apple seems to know this is a sore spot for privacy-centric users, so we’ll see how well they take to it when the Series 12 watches hit the scene later this month. —Kyle Barr Both the exterior and interior displays of the iPhone Duo rely on a 1:4 aspect ratio. That’s very different than what you’re used to with most candy bar-style phones, but it also means these devices are much, much better for watching content you don’t get on TikTok. Apple showed the device playing games at its full-screen height without any black bars around the content. For movies, it’s going to get interesting. Despite some dubious X post you may have seen, IMAX films use either a 1.90:1 or 1.43:1 aspect ratio. Sure, that fits the Duo’s screen better than you would on a regular mobile phone, but it would still require some black bars to make it fit. Did Christopher Nolan ever want you to watch The Odyssey on your phone? I imagine the very idea would give him a migraine. —Kyle Barr BREAKING: Apple's Polishing Cloth is compatible with the iPhone Duo, iPhone 18 Pro, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4/Series 12 pic.twitter.com/0yxMME2qur — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 9, 2026 Okay, everybody calm down. It’s official, your Apple polishing cloth (which recently had its price slashed to $9) is indeed compatible with both the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo. Go ahead and feel free to smooth that folding phone until it’s as smooth as glass. Oh wait, it’s already made of metal and glass. Whatever, just keep scrubbing. Apple commands it. —Kyle Barr How much are you willing to pay for the return of the Ceramic Apple Watch? A Series 12 ceramic model starts at $809 at the 42mm size in either pearl white or night blue colorways. The watches come with both GPS and cellular connectivity, but they’re easily the most expensive version of the Series 12. Meanwhile, an Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $719. —Kyle Barr Burgundy happens to be my favorite color, which means, of course, I’m very smitten with the iPhone 18 Pro. Burgundy is also a modern region in France that’s today known for its wine-making. During the Medieval period, it was a duchy that proved to be one of the most important regions for the late Medieval political field. In the 15th century, Duke Charles the Bold tried his damndest to create an independent kingdom of Burgundy through diplomacy and war. He was a known patron of the arts, and his nascent kingdom also became a center of chivalric etiquette. Unfortunately, Chrales’ dream of a revived Burgundian kingdom died at the Battle of Nancy against the Swiss Confederation. Still, Burgundy lives on thanks to Charles’s epic motto, “Je L’ay Emprins,” which translates to “I have dared it.” —Kyle Barr It’s THIN. It’s VERSATILE It’s DURABLE. It fits in your pocket. And it FOLDS. Meet iPhone Duo. pic.twitter.com/lVpBmC36hx — Greg Joswiak (@gregjoz) September 9, 2026 All the videos showcasing the iPhone Duo include this slick-looking animation where it seems the exterior screen bleeds over into the interior display. I want to believe this is how it will look in-person, but there’s another side of me that wonders if the look of this animation will depend on whether you’re staring at the device straight-on. Also, I want to know if it works on other apps, not just the home screen. —Kyle Barr Netflix made a special version of its app for the iPhone Duo that makes use of both the exterior and interior displays. On the outside, you’ll scroll through clips from some of the streamer’s shows, and then opening it up, you’ll be greeted with a larger screen-filling video. Apple does want you to use its device for watching shows and content, though it’s also partnered with Zoom and Slack for making use of the larger 7.58-inch interior display. —Kyle Barr Apple imagines you’ll treat your iPhone Duo like a miniature, pocketable tablet. That makes sense, given the Apple Pencil compatibility and the consistent bezels. To that end, Apple’s also making a Folio case for the Duo with a built-in gumstick kickstand. It also covers up the exterior screen in this mode, but you weren’t looking at it anyway. The Folio case is only available in a tan taupe color and navy blue. —Kyle Barr iPhone Duo prices. $3200 for 2TB model. pic.twitter.com/aopePNw1nx — Mark Gurman (@markgurman) September 9, 2026 Foldable phones are expensive—there’s no doubt about that—but if you want the top-of-the-line iPhone Duo, you’re going to have to really shell out. The iPhone Duo with 2TB of storage costs $3,200 before tax, which is a ton of money (but somehow less than a Vision Pro). Still, I think I speak for most wallets when I say… ouch. —James Pero Apple says that, starting Sept. 14, you’ll be able to download the next OS update to all your Apple devices, including iOS 27, macOS 27 Golden Gate, watchOS 27, and so on. Just know that all the new Siri AI capabilities are still listed as a “beta,” which is how Apple plans to wash its hands when the chatbot inevitably makes a mistake. Additionally, some anticipated features, like the Apple Watch “Audio Intelligence” features, won’t be available until later. —Kyle Barr The new Apple Watch doesn’t seem all that different from the Series 11, at least on the surface. Beyond a whole slew of new health metric tracking, the big additions are all in how these watches now include extra AI features that use audio capture. The most important ones you’ll get to know are “Siri Recap” and “Live Rewind.” Siri can use your data and combine that with your audio to give you a rundown of what you did that day. Live Rewind can enable users to see a summary of what somebody just said to you when you weren’t listening. Those specific features won’t be available until a beta comes out this October. —Kyle Barr That foldable iPhone won’t be available until Oct. 23, more than a month after the iPhone 18 Pro hits the scene. Preorders start Oct. 16. Here’s the big news: the iPhone Duo will start at $1,999. At the very least, $2,000 is a lot less than the $2,500 rumors originally suggested. —Kyle Barr Apple’s new C2 modem supports 5G mmWave. For reference, previous modems, the C1 and C1X, both in-house products, didn’t have that. Apple says the C2 also allows for 50% faster uploads, which is nothing to scoff at. —James Pero The iPhone Duo is using a special screen layer that Apple promises is doing a few things, but the most important aspect is how it may reduce the chance you’ll see the crease. We’ll have to see that for ourselves, considering the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 starts life with minimal crease, but it becomes more apparent the more you open it up. —Kyle Barr Naturally, multitasking on the iPhone Duo looks very iPad-esque. You can stack apps vertically or horizontally, and it looks like there’s some intuitive dragging and dropping. In a way, Apple has been making foldable phone software for years, just not on a foldable phone. —James Pero Apple says using the iPhone Duo won’t be restricted to your digits. You’ll be able to use an Apple Pencil with USB-c on the interior or exterior screen. However, Apple makes no mention of the more versatile Apple Pencil Pro, which may remain only usable on an iPad. —Kyle Barr Apple’s first foldable phone also has a FaceTime camera built into the screen on the right side when it’s opened up. This means you can have your phone open and have multiple people take up different parts of the screen. What we really want is to take video calls while—hopefully—being able to keep using your device. —Kyle Barr There’s a whole lot of new features coming to Apple Watch Series 12, but at least it doesn’t cost any more than before. It starts at $399 and now—finally—comes with ceramic options. —Kyle Barr Apple has two new versions of AirPods 5. Both have better ANC, but only the more expensive model has swipe controls and wireless charging. You’ll also have to shell out more money for one more hour of battery life. The base model gets four hours with ANC on, and the more expensive model gets five hours with ANC on. —James Pero Look at those specs. As you might’ve expected, the Watch Series 12 is better in basically every way imaginable, with better sensors, of course. —Matt Wille Apple’s updated AI will now synthesize all your health information, like sleep data, exercise, and heart rate, and give you a “Health Age” score. What if I don’t actually want to know that much about myself? —Matt Wille The new Apple Watch will take your heart rate up to 24x more than its predecessor. Apple says it’s now the “most accurate heart rate sensing” available in a wearable. —Matt Wille The AirPods 5 now feature better ANC, which promises around five hours of battery life thanks to a reengineered power cell. And despite everything getting more expensive, they still cost the same $129 as the AirPods 4. The AirPods 5 with a wireless charging case will now cost $149. —Kyle Barr That’s right, RAMageddon has come for the iPhone. The new iPhone 18 Pro will start at $1,200, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max will ask for $1,300. That’s both $100 more than the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, respectively. Let’s just admit that—considering today’s memory prices—it could have been way worse. —Kyle Barr Apple’s planning to support Google’s SynthID watermarks for AI-generated images, but it’s now also trying to beat deepfakes with a reference photo future. Essentially, Apple will host an original image in its Private Cloud Compute servers that doesn’t have any modifications. —Kyle Barr The iPhone Pro’s camera is getting more professional with additional controls. Now, with Pro Camera controls, you can adjust things like aperture, white balance, shutter speed, and more. The Pro controls also work with video, allowing you to adjust shutter speed for more motion blur. You can also maintain focus on moving subjects with AI. For anyone who takes iPhone photography seriously, I assume these will be pretty rad. —James Pero But it’s still pretty damn cool. Apple has added a mechanical aperture to its 48-megapixel main “fusion” camera lens, which means that you’ll have much more control over depth of field for your shots. It’s going to be a very pro-centric feature, but at least it’s one of those features that will potentially make amateur photogs more willing to reach for their phone instead of their camera in a pinch. —Kyle Barr The iPhone 18 Pro is supposed to offer much better performance, and a big reason for that is because the iPhone should be much better at keeping cool. Apple said the phone now has a 3X larger vapor chamber, which is important because the redesigned A20 chip now has its silicon die placed next to its memory, which means the 2nm chip can seat closer to the thermal system. All this means that, maybe—finally—the iPhone 18 won’t be as toasty as usual. —Kyle Barr The A20 Pro is Apple’s newest high-end iPhone chip and comes with two “neural engines.” That equates to quite a few improvements, according to Apple, including “2x more compute.” There’s also a 50% increase in memory bandwidth. Whether you really feel the results will depend on what you’re doing, of course, but it looks impressive on paper. —James Pero Apple mentioned that some of Siri’s capabilities may be rate limited but didn’t offer more details during its event. We’ll just have to find out for ourselves if Apple wants us to buy into an iCloud subscription to get the most use out of AI. —Kyle Barr Siri’s AI enhancements are finally here. They were in the latest betas, but if you’ve been waiting for the full release, know that Siri has more “personal context” that allows it to understand what you’ve been posting in your emails or messages, and it can take some actions on your behalf. Siri also has several “expressive” options for voice, but only on the more recent iPhone models. This has all been well-established since WWDC, but we’ll see how well it performs on the millions of iPhones that can use it. —Kyle Barr There it is: Burgundy is the new color for the iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. Other colors for the iPhone 18 Pro: Deep Black, Glacier (light blue), and a new silver. The glass panel on the backside is also color-matched to the aluminum frame. —Raymond Wong iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Check out the new color with color matched back. Burgundy is the new color#appleevent pic.twitter.com/1maaD28lsw — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 John Ternus really had us going there for a second. “Intelligent Personal Hub?” I mean, come on, we were all thinking smart home hub, right? —James Pero While the folks in Cupertino, California are greeting John Ternus, the rest of us plebs watching the livestream are greeted with a very Apple-ish opening trailer, or perhaps multiple trailers. And suddenly, Tim Cook’s voice, then Tim Cook, who reveals he’s no longer the head honcho. It’s John Ternus, y’all. They’re really making a big deal out of this. —Kyle Barr Ternus didn’t say the signature “Good Morning,” like Tim Cook always did. Guess he’s doing things his own way. He said Apple has been doing a lot of imagining and we’ll see some of those things today. —Raymond Wong John Ternus is out on stage and attendees gave him a loud ovation. So much love for the new guy. —Raymond Wong Standing ovation for John Ternus! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/kXPDk3NLNt — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 New Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! Where is John Ternus? Probably behind the stage getting ready to hop on and “Good Morning” us all. —Raymond Wong New Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook sighted! #appleevent pic.twitter.com/KMQXtQWqMs — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Thanks to the iPhone 17 Pro’s 8x zoom, I was able to scope on Apple’s head of marketing Greg Joswiak and chief of software engineering, Craig Federighi. Dude’s hair still still looks incredible. Gotta find out what conditioner he uses to get that kinda volume. —Raymond Wong I spy Craig Federighi and Greg Jozwiak at the #appleevent pic.twitter.com/QAW9wUSz64 — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 I’m seated inside of the Steve Jobs Theater. If you’ve never been here, know this: the theater has plush leather (?!) seats, outlets for each one, and the speaker system is one of the very best I’ve ever experienced. —Raymond Wong 15 minutes until the #appleevent keynote! pic.twitter.com/Cpjopg4iIT — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Apple’s new leader woke up super early and shared this teaser to his X account. But what is it? The variable aperture for the iPhone 18 Pro Max? Some glimpse of a close-up of the foldable iPhone? Make your guesses in the comments. —Raymond Wong — John Ternus (@johnternus) September 9, 2026 Here’s my food review of the breakfast for invited media: B. I’m wolfing down this mini chocolate croissant and an apple tart. I’m going to need the sugar to power me through the long day. The coffee is mid, too. Edible, but nothing special. I’m old enough to remember when the food and drinks situation was amazing. Of course, this was in the early days when the Steve Jobs Theater had just opened. —Raymond Wong We just picked up our badges and have arrived at the Steve Jobs Theater. The current temperature is 72 degrees Fahrenheit in Cupertino, and it’s supposed to reach a high of 96 degrees by the late afternoon. I’m definitely feeling a bit antsy, but I can’t wait to see the so-called iPhone Duo. Is this the foldable that will make foldable phones mainstream? We shall see. —Raymond Wong Got my #AppleEvent badge! Ready to see the foldable iPhone pic.twitter.com/vhcDNwJoVH — Ray Wong (@raywongy) September 9, 2026 Maybe I should have stuck to my prediction that Apple will call the foldable iPhone the “iPhone Duo.” Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman said on X last night that he believes Apple has decided to call it the iPhone Duo, with the device starting at $2,000 and shipping in September. A storage option with 2TB could cost around $3,000 he said. The Apple sleuth also said that the iPhone Duo will support Apple Pencil and launch in dark blue and white colorways. John Ternus could do the funniest thing ever and not call it the iPhone Duo just to screw with Gurman, though. That would be pretty funny. —Raymond Wong Well, no regular iPhones, that is. Rumor has it Apple will only be announcing the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max today, with no iPhone 18 in the mix. It’s an interesting choice from Apple, a company that usually hopes to offer something lower-end for users who aren’t ready to shell out $1,000+ on a new phone. But hey, we are expecting to see the foldable iPhone today. That’s basically two phones in one, right? —Matt Wille Apple has just released a firmware update for a product that does not exist yet Beats 360 Firmware 4A203 is out. It confirms the Beats 360 name and the 4 colors: Black, Pink, White, Cloud It also includes HD images of the upcoming products pic.twitter.com/a24FDZcu1m — Aaron (@aaronp613) September 8, 2026 AirPods aren’t the only audio product that should be on your Apple radar right now. According to leaks, Beats has a new pair of wireless headphones in the works called the Beats 360. There are even some HD images leaked along with them, and they look… very Beats-y. Whether these are announced at today’s event is another story, but the timing of the leak is certainly interesting. —James Pero Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are likely going to cost at least $100 more, according to Bloomberg’s ever-consistent Apple leaker Mark Gurman. So what kinds of hardware upgrades will Apple try to suggest are worth the ballooning cost of memory? Gurman says there should be some big camera upgrades this year that will include a mechanical aperture on at least one of the new lenses. This grants more fine-tuned control over your photos, and it may be my main reason for personally opting for the bar-style phone instead of the upcoming foldable. The other big upgrade may be Apple’s downsizing of the Dynamic Island. It could appear smaller on your phone without any content on it, but Gurman suggested users will be able to toggle between up to three live activities at one time. Compared to something like the relatively pointless Camera Control switch, the Dynamic Island has proved itself a worthwhile feature over time, and it’s nice to see it with more usability. —Kyle Barr It’s looking like AirPods with cameras in them are a long shot on today’s laundry list of releases, but AirPods 5 might make an appearance. According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, AirPods 5 will bring a few perks over the last generation, including better active noise cancellation (ANC). There will be two models, according to Gurman, and one of them will have wireless charging in the case while the other won’t. Sure, it’s not as mind-blowing as wireless earbuds that can remember where you left your keys, but it’s something. —James Pero You shouldn’t expect any massive hardware update from Apple’s wearables this year. Instead, the main reason Apple wants you to be excited may be for new software updates—and of course that means AI. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman suggested The Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 will have a feature that summarizes your day, and that may include conversations. This AI Siri-enabled feature may be called “Recaps,” according to Gurman. The big question is whether Apple will have it run all the live-long day or if you can set it to only start recording at certain times or in certain locations. Apple will, of course, try to emphasize how it will keep your data secure, but I don’t imagine many users are still that enticed by more self-surveillance features. Also, don’t expect this feature to come to any past Apple Watches, which is especially annoying considering how many recent Apple Watch models can’t even get watchOS 27. —Kyle Barr One of the less-anticipated product reveals for the “Surprise and Shine” event on Wednesday may be a new version of the Apple TV 4K set-top box. It’s a good thing too, since the old one was looking a little long in the tooth. A new box necessitates a new processor upgrade, and MacRumors claims—based on some pre-release code—that we may see an A19 or A19 Pro chip. This six-core SoC was first built for the iPhone 17 generation, but that means Apple may also be upgrading the RAM spec from 4GB to 8GB or more. We’d hate to see what that does to the price. A current-gen Apple TV 4K went from $130 to $200 in Apple’s big across-the-board price hike back in June. —Kyle Barr We’ve been reading purported details about the foldable iPhone, iPhone 18 Pros, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5 for months now. Here are all the major rumors on what to expect from John Ternus and company tomorrow. Spoiler alert: it’s full of spoilers! —Raymond Wong Guys, I’ve been in Cupertino for 24 hours, and let me tell you, it’s dry out here. I’m very excited to see Apple’s first foldable iPhone. Can’t say the same about my skin drying up. Today is a planning day with the Consumer Tech Team. We’re gonna be working like maniacs to bring you all fast and accurate coverage of everything that Apple announces tomorrow. —Raymond Wong

item.title: iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Upgrade for the Cameras
item.description:
Source: Gizmodo Score: 2.69
You’re going to end up squinting long and hard at the new iPhone 18 Pro to spot the differences between the new and previous generations. To save your eyes, I’m here to give you the breakdown of what’s actually changed. TL;DR: you’re going to care if you’ve always wanted more control over your phone’s cameras or a phone that doesn’t get as hot as quickly. Of course, the other major differentiator is the launch price. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro now start at $1,200 and $1,300, respectively. They’re both $100 more than what the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max cost in 2025. That’s a symptom of the ongoing RAM shortage, and Apple has already increased the price of its iPhone Air and iPhone 17e just after it revealed its iPhone 18 at Wednesday’s event. If we’re being honest, the biggest change this year is more what this means for the iPhone lineup. First, the new, most expensive device in Apple’s newly announced cellular lineup is the iPhone Duo, a wide foldable that takes the cake as the largest shakeup in iPhones since—well—ever. It’s a device built for media consumption, whereas the iPhone 18 Pro is relegated as the “professional” level device for people who really want the best phone pics. Also, Apple has decided to hold off launching a new regular iPhone 18 this month. It may save it for next year, when it debuts an iPhone 18e budget device and—possibly—an iPhone Air 2. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Colors Goodbye, Cosmic Orange. The new leading color for 2026 is a dark red burgundy. It’s not exactly the kind of color that creates a slew of tone-matched accessories like orange did, though it’s certainly more obvious than some past devices like the iPhone 14 Pro’s ultra-dark purple.
