In addition, the iPhone 18 Pro also comes in a muted “glacier” blue, a silver colorway, and—finally—an actual black, rather than some dark gray. It may be a semi-controversial take, but I never liked the look of the iPhone 17 Pro’s orange. It was too bright, too in your face, and way too trendy. Burgundy happens to be my favorite color—not the least because of the interesting history behind the area of Burgundy in France. I guess we’re setting up a war between the Prince of Orange in the Netherlands and the Duke of Burgundy, but I digress. Apple is also color-matching the back glass to the phone itself, whereas the iPhone 17 Pro’s back glass appeared a lighter shade than the rest of the device. Apple is sticking with aluminum sides for this generation—a decision that still rankles some who miss the sturdier titanium frame. Just like the previous generation, the front glass is still using Ceramic Shield 2, while the back panel is base Ceramic Shield. They’re still sturdy devices and are rated IP68 for dust resistance and survivability in water up to 6 meters for 30 minutes. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Screen If you’re comparing each generation’s screen, you’ll first notice the iPhone 18 Pro has a shrunken Dynamic Island. That’s because Apple managed to stick its infrared camera—used for FaceID—behind the screen. Now, the Dynamic Island is 25% smaller when not in use, but it can expand to include up to three live activities at once. The iPhone 18 Pro is still sporting a 6.3-inch OLED display, while the Max version boosts that size to 6.9 inches. Each model supports the usual ProMotion up to 120Hz of refresh rate, the same as the iPhone 17 Pro. You could stare at each screen for hours and find there’s essentially no difference between the past and new generations of slab phones. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Internals The phones’ internals are where things get interesting. First up, Apple’s new phone is breaking through with its first 2nm chip, the A20 Pro. Compared to the 3nm A19 Pro inside the iPhone 17 Pro, the smaller die size leads to better efficiency. The six-core CPU also integrates neural accelerators to handle all the new Apple Intelligence and Siri AI tasks in iOS 27. Apple also claims the CPU has 50% more memory bandwidth than the A19 Pro. To assist with that AI, there’s also a new dual-16-core neural engine. GPU-wise, Apple claims it’s given the new phone a big boost. It’s supposed to be 40% faster than the previous generation, so that could be a big boon if you were looking to game on your phone. Apple has also reengineered its chips so it packages the processor die close to the phone’s memory, reducing latency and allowing it to sit directly on the newly redesigned vapor chamber. The extra capabilities of this new chip would mean Apple has to do more to keep these phones running well. As to that, the company says it created a new vapor chamber that supposedly has 3X more surface area than the iPhone 17 Pro’s. Not only is that chamber supposed to aid with cooling, it may greatly enhance sustained performance by 40%. These all seem like small things, but these internal additions add up. As a final note, Apple is including its N1 Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 chip in both the Pro and Pro Max phones—same as last year. However, this year the Pro and Pro Max chips now sport different modems. The iPhone 18 Pro contains the new C2 cellular modem, which Apple says is more efficient than the C1. However, the iPhone 18 Pro Max doesn’t have a listed modem in its spec sheet. As first noted by MacRumors, the two phones have different LTE bands, which indicates they’re not running the same exact chip setup. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Battery The improvements to the iPhone 18 Pro chip are significant, though they may not play out into huge performance improvements if you’re already used to the iPhone 17 Pro. What may be more grokable is that if you jump from 17 Pro to 18 Pro, there is an increased battery life. The new eSIM-only models contain a 4,288 mAh capacity battery, slightly larger than the previous generation’s 4,252 mAh. In reality, it’s the efficiency claims that are doing the most for battery life. Apple claims you’ll be able to get iPhone 17 Pro Max battery life on a regular iPhone 18 Pro. Meanwhile, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is supposed to have the best longevity of any iPhone ever. Apple claims you can get 36 hours on a non-Max iPhone 18 Pro during video playback tests, but those don’t matter one bit compared to real-life scenarios. Again, this is something we’ll have to test ourselves. Both phones also support ultra-fast charging, with the iPhone 18 Pro Max meant to hit 50% battery in 30 minutes. It’s essentially equivalent to what we had on the iPhone 17 Pro. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Camera Apple explicitly wants you to know the iPhone 18 Pro is its camera phone. For the first time, Apple’s adding a mechanical aperture to its main 48-megapixel wide lens, allowing up to four f-stops of f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0. Those settings can drastically change your camera’s depth of field as well as how you can light and frame your subjects. Samsung previously tried this on its Galaxy S9 and S10 series, though those phones only allowed for either a wide-open or f/2.4 aperture. China-centric phones like the Xiaomi 14 Ultra include variable apertures between f/1.63 and f/4.0. Still, this is a new capability that no previous iPhone could claim. Most regular phone users will stick with automatic settings. On the flip side of things, if you were actually interested in understanding more about how photographers understand cameras, the iPhone 18 Pro could be your first taste. Google’s latest camera capabilities in devices like the Pixel 11 Pro are all focused on software for photo processing. Somehow, it’s Apple who’s trying to give its users more fine-tuned control. The iPhone 18 Pro still has three lenses: a 48-megapixel Fusion wide lens, a 48-megapixel Fusion periscope telephoto lens, and a 48-megapixel Fusion ultra-wide lens. Other than a variable aperture, not much has otherwise changed. Apple said it has upgraded its photo processing pipeline to help it produce better photos. Apple also added new “Pro” controls to the camera app to finally give all the “shot on iPhone” people more manual options for their photos and video—such as shutter speed or white balance. iPhone 18 Pro vs. iPhone 17 Pro: Software features The iPhone 17 Pro is perfectly capable of running all the newfangled iOS 27 features, including Siri AI. However, there’s at least one other iPhone 18 Pro-exclusive feature: Apple Reference Image. The phone will essentially take your photo and process it through Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers to create an unalterable reference photo. If somebody takes your shot or deepfakes it, you’ll be able to compare theirs to your original. Other than that, iPhone 17 Pro users may have very few reasons to upgrade. The main focus this year is on cameras, and if you only got your “Pro”-level phone for clout, then there’s not much here for you to care about. However, for those of us waiting for the most powerful iPhone, this one certainly fits the bill. Also, if—like me—you were dreaming of a Pro-level iPhone in red, burgundy may be the closest we’ll ever get. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are up for preorder Sept. 12, and they should start shipping Sept. 18.

item.title: Android's private DNS feature solves a problem most people don't know they have
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.69
If you care about protecting your privacy online, you've probably seen an ad for VPNs. You likely also know to seek out private messaging apps like Signal and Proton Mail. But there's another change you need to make in order to protect your phone's web traffic from prying eyes, and it's a relatively simple fix. Your DNS isn't private by default It's time to change this DNS stands for Domain Name System. It's what enables you to get somewhere by typing a website name rather than having to enter an exact numerical IP address. Without DNS, typing howtogeek.com would only yield an error message. Out of the box, your phone's DNS activity is quite likely neither encrypted nor private. Your internet service provider (such as Comcast or Verizon) or carrier (Verizon, T-Mobile, or AT&T) can see every site you visit. If you’re on a public Wi-Fi network, you run the risk of a snoop taking a peek at your activities as well. Third-party DNS providers like Cloudflare, NextDNS, and Mullvad offer a way to browse the web while hiding your domain name requests from your ISP. It does so by encrypting your DNS activity, just as encrypted email masks the content of your messages and HTTPS hides what data a website is transmitting to your device. How to enable Private DNS on Android It only takes a couple taps To keep your phone from leaking your domain name requests, you'll need to dive into your network settings. You can do so by swiping down from the top of the screen and tapping on the gear icon that opens your phone's Settings app. Then navigate to "Network & internet." Towards the bottom, you'll see an option for "Private DNS." Tapping here provides you with three options: Off, Automatic, and Private DNS provider hostname. You’ll likely see “Automatic” enabled by default, which means your phone will use DNS encryption when it detects the option available. This leaves you at the whim of your ISP or carrier, who may prefer to track and monetize your browsing activity rather than protect it. “Off” disables DNS encryption entirely. For a continuous private connection, you'll want to select a private DNS provider hostname, and you will then need to enter an address in order for the changes to take effect. If you don't yet know one to put here, you can find several options in our list of the best DNS servers for secure browsing. Just keep in mind that you will need to enter a hostname into this field, not an IP address. In other words, you’ll need to enter the private web address your provider offers, rather than a series of numbers and periods. Once you've entered your selection, you can confirm whether things are working using the Safer.com Browser Privacy Test. That said, there are circumstances where this fix may not be the one you’re looking for, and you’d actually be better off leaving the default setting in place. Private DNS does not fully mask your web activity There is still a lot your ISP can learn about you DNS encryption, whether via DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT), doesn’t fully prevent your ISP from seeing what you do online. While you’re shielding your DNS lookups, all the traffic that follows still happens over their connection. This means the ISP can see the destination IP address you connected to and how much data was transmitted. The company can also see how much time you spend on the site before switching to another. You’ll need to take other steps if you sincerely wish to prevent others from gaining insights into what you do online. The more technically minded who are interested in self-hosting can rent a cheap VPS, install Wireguard, and tell all of their devices to use this VPS as a full-tunnel VPN endpoint. Those of us who aren’t interested in that whole song and dance can look into commercial VPN options. They often provide mobile apps that make encrypting a connection as simple as possible, often requiring only a single tap and granting some permissions. Just know that if you opt to use a commercial VPN, such as Private Internet Access or ProtonVPN, they tend to offer their own encrypted DNS. In that situation, you’ll want to leave the private DNS setting on your phone set to “Automatic” and trust the VPN connection to shield your DNS lookups instead. There’s no way to go online without leaking at least a little Private DNS encrypts your DNS lookups, but it doesn’t mask the resulting web traffic. VPNs may go a step further, but your ISP can tell you’re using one, and you must trust your VPN provider not to abuse your trust. It’s even possible to tell someone is using TOR, even if that may be all you’re able to tell. In other words, don’t start browsing the web with the false assumption that everything you do is private, but by reducing your online footprint as best you can, you reduce how much information can be monetized or used for online attacks.

item.title: My Android notifications kept arriving late—these settings were the problem
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 5.23
I've had problems with Android notifications arriving late for years. Usually, it's not a huge deal—if someone needs me urgently, they'll just call instead of texting me. But not all notifications are equal. An Instagram Reel shared by my friend can wait an hour for a reaction, but an important work email about a meeting that's been canceled or moved up a few hours can't. Since I can't afford to miss notifications like those anymore, I finally decided to figure out what was causing the delays and fix the problem. Battery Saver is delaying your notifications Battery life comes at a cost Some people like to keep Battery Saver (aka Power Saving Mode on some devices) permanently enabled on their devices for a few good reasons. Modern phones are plenty fast, so sacrificing a fraction of a second for apps to load to extend the battery life of your phone by up to a few hours is a worthwhile tradeoff. However, on top of throttling the CPU's maximum clock speed and disabling various other performance optimizations to reduce power draw, Battery Saver actually does a number of other things to your phone. The most important thing for us today is that it heavily restricts or outright stops background sync for non-essential apps. Some apps might work just fine, but others might fail to sync for hours. Fortunately, the fix is super easy. Head over to Settings > Battery and disable Battery Saver or switch to Balanced mode, depending on what brand your phone is. Battery optimization is stopping apps from syncing in the background Give specific apps more freedom Android has a pretty clever feature that optimizes battery use on a per-app basis. It allows your phone to throttle apps you don't use and prioritize background activity for your most-used ones. It's a pretty clever system for the most part, but it's also one of the most common sources of delayed notifications because apps are optimized by default. This includes your email app of choice, Slack, Asana, and other important work-related apps that you might only use for a few minutes a day but can't afford to miss notifications from. At the same time, social media apps will probably get more priority if that's what you use the most on your phone. Fortunately, you can adjust this default behavior fairly easily. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps. Find an app on this list that's experiencing delayed notifications and tap on Battery usage, then switch it from Optimized to Unrestricted. The exact wording varies from brand to brand, but since it's built directly into Android, the setting is there—and it's most likely what's causing your delayed notifications. Your app is being cut off from the internet in the background Let your important apps use data Data Saver is another core Android feature that optimizes cellular data usage. It's disabled by default, but if you enabled it at some point and forgot to turn it back off, you might not even be aware of it. Some phones display a persistent notification at the top, but not all (or the option to do so might be disabled by default). In any case, it only takes a few seconds to check. Go to Settings > Network and Internet (or equivalent) > Data usage > Data Saver and disable the feature. If you must keep it on because you're on a limited plan, there's an option to leave data unrestricted for some apps, which is the perfect compromise. Again, the wording differs between brands, so just poke around until you find it. Android is restricting an app you haven't opened lately Even unused apps deserve notification access Pause app activity if unused is another semi-problematic core Android feature that was introduced with Android 12. It's surprisingly aggressive at what it does: it puts an app into complete hibernation, kills notifications, revokes permissions, and wipes cache data if it hasn't been used in 3 months. This can be problematic if the app in question is something you access very infrequently but still need to keep up with, like a specific smart home app, security alert app, travel app, or similar. Unfortunately, there's no global setting to switch off app hibernation, but what you can do is disable it on an app-by-app basis. Go to Settings > Apps > See all apps, find the app you suspect got disabled, and disable Pause app activity if unused. On my phone, it's the Manage unused apps toggle that needs to be turned off. Like with the settings I discussed previously, the exact wording might differ between brands, but if your phone runs Android 12 or newer, it's there. A manufacturer-specific setting is restricting apps on its own Your phone might have a hidden battery saver Everything I've discussed so far has been general fixes that you can use on every Android phone. However, some brands have their own additional battery management features and optimizations on top of those built into Android. Unfortunately, since there are so many brands and things are constantly changing with updates, going over all of them here could quickly turn into its own article. So, if you're still experiencing delayed notifications after trying all of the fixes above, I recommend doing a little research on your specific device to see if there's a hidden toggle or feature that you can change to force background sync for problematic apps. Most notification delays have a simple explanation I'm sure that most Android owners can relate to the frustration of delayed notifications that happen here and there. The majority of the time, the cause is some data- or battery-saving feature that's built into Android, and luckily, the fix is often as simple as changing a single option.

item.title: There's a tiny computer hiding in most USB-C cables (and it isn't always used for good)
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 4.43
Two USB-C cables can look identical, cost wildly different amounts, and behave nothing alike. The reason sits inside the connector housing: a chip that talks to your devices before any power moves. It's genuinely useful engineering. It's also a convenient place to hide something nasty. What is that tiny computer about? The e-marker chip that negotiates power and speed The component is called an e-marker, short for electronically marked cable, and it lives inside the connector shell rather than the cable itself. It communicates with chargers and devices over the Configuration Channel (CC) pin, telling connected hardware what the cable can actually do. It draws its own power from the VCONN pin—up to about a watt—which is what lets a passive-looking cable participate actively in a negotiation without any external supply. That negotiation happens before anything else. Power Delivery transactions begin by addressing the cable itself in a stage known as SOP prime, and only once the cable's capabilities are established does the rest of the process continue between source and sink. The chip publishes its specification as a set of 32-bit values called Vendor Defined Objects, or VDOs, covering things like the manufacturer and model, the signalling protocol and maximum transfer speed, whether the cable's controller can communicate independently with the charger or device, and the hardware and firmware version. Not every cable has one. Cables rated at or below 3A aren't required to carry an e-marker chip; anything expected to handle more current needs one. In practice, a cable carries an e-marker if it is rated above USB 2.0 speeds or above 60W. Either one, not necessarily both. Given that USB Power Delivery now reaches 240W, and that pushing that much energy down an unrated cable risks overheating or fire, the chip functions as a safety mechanism as much as a feature flag. Plug in a cable with no chip and both ends assume the worst case, capping you at 60W and 480Mbps regardless of what your laptop and charger are capable of. What are its downsides? Opaque specifications and a perfect hiding place The first problem is honesty. Charging capability and data capability are separate fields in the e-marker, and manufacturers set them independently: a genuine, spec-compliant 240W cable can declare its data capability as 480Mbps, the same speed as a cable from 2001. Buyers reasonably assume that an expensive, high-wattage cable is also a fast one. The chip cheerfully says otherwise, in a format nobody without a protocol analyzer can read. The second problem is worse. If a connector housing can accommodate a microcontroller, flash storage and firmware, it can accommodate other things. Security researcher Mike Grover built the O.MG cable as a penetration-testing tool for red teams and awareness training. Hidden inside the connector is a web server, a keylogger and a keystroke-injection engine reachable over Wi-Fi, so the cable can type commands, capture what's typed back, and be driven remotely from across the room. Elite models store up to 650,000 keystrokes, support geofencing to trigger payloads by location, and can self-destruct to render the cable inert. In December 2024, industrial CT scanner manufacturer Lumafield imaged an O.MG cable and found sophisticated electronics and an antenna packed into the connector, alongside a second set of wires connecting a secondary die hidden beneath the primary microcontroller. Those bond wires are roughly the thickness of a human hair, and the arrangement would evade inspection techniques that can't assess an assembly volumetrically. Even an X-ray image can't reliably show whether a cable has been tampered with, because the additional electronics are so small and so cleverly integrated that they're nearly indistinguishable from regular components. Should you worry? Real risk, modest odds, and defenses worth knowing Proportion matters here. No real-world juice jacking attack has ever been publicly documented, though researchers keep proving it's technically possible, most notably at USENIX Security 2025, where Graz University of Technology researchers presented ChoiceJacking, the first family of USB attacks to bypass existing juice jacking mitigations by injecting input events while a data connection is being established. It let a malicious charger spoof user input and enable data transfer or code execution on eleven Android and iOS devices without consent. Apple and Google have since shipped fixes in iOS 18.4 and Android 15, and on current iPhones connecting a new USB device requires a passcode or Face ID. The standards body's answer has existed for years and gone largely unused. The USB-IF launched its Type-C Authentication Program with 128-bit cryptographic verification of chargers, devices, cables and power sources, managed through DigiCert. It remains optional, with no mandatory requirement for OEMs to adopt it. Practical defense is therefore about provenance rather than detection. Use your own cables, buy from the manufacturer or an authorized seller, and label what's yours. Keep your phone locked when charging in public and decline connection prompts you didn't initiate. A Malicious Cable Detector exists for around $40, using side-channel power analysis to flag the electrical signature of an implant, but its own documentation frames it as a first-line screen rather than a forensic instrument, and it can never prove a cable is clean. Weight and feel tell you nothing. Cables are computers now, so treat them accordingly The e-marker exists for good reasons, and it makes modern fast charging possible. But it normalized the idea of silicon inside a connector, which is exactly what makes malicious implants so hard to spot. Buy your own cables, from people you trust.

item.title: Loaded dice, card cheaters, and other unethical board game parts you can 3D print
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 3.08
The great thing about 3D printers is that they can make almost anything these days. The bad thing about 3D printers is that you can make almost anything with them. There are some obvious, actually illegal things that will get you in trouble if you print them. Though I won't mention them here, you can get on a watchlist on your own without my help! Then there are things that are legal, but they're a bad idea to 3D print. But what about things that aren't necessarily illegal, and are technically fine to print, but are also really unethical? Loaded dice If you've seen the movie "Casino", you know to leave these at home In case you somehow don't know, "loaded" dice are designed to fall on a specific number almost every time. In a fair die, there's an equal chance of landing on any given number, but if you change the weight distribution of the die to favor a specific number on the bottom, then you can control which number shows at the top. Traditionally, this is done using metal weights inside the dice, but with a 3D printer, where you can design the interior structure precisely, all you have to do is determine where the weight of the infill is. Indeed, with RevK's Loaded Dice, you need to set the infill density to 95% for it to work, and there are six models in total, each favoring a different potential number. Given how light PLA is, it's not really obvious that these dice don't have a uniform weight distribution. But a much larger issue would be that the dice were 3D-printed in the first place. So it's not like you're going to surreptitiously switch these out for store-bought fair dice. That said, people are getting really good at processing 3D prints so that you can't even tell they were made with a 3D printer. ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 - Build Volume - 256 × 256 × 256 mm - Connectivity - Wi-Fi The ELEGOO Centauri Carbon 2 builds on the solid foundation of its predecessor and adds an affordable, effective multicolor system to the mix. - Heated Build Plate - Yes - Top Print Speed - ≤500 mm/s - Max Plate Temperature - 110°C - Max Print Temperature - 350°C - MULTICOLOR PRINTING - Yes A card shuffler that deliberately deals winning hands Though, to be fair, you need more than just a 3D printer for this one! You may have heard (as reported by the BBC) of those rigged high-stakes underground poker games involving NBA players and lots of high-tech cheating equipment. Well, if you look into it, you'll see that part of the scam involved a modified casino-grade card shuffler. This device is supposed to ensure a fair deal in games like Texas Hold'em, but by hacking and modifying the device, you can precisely determine where any given card is at any time. Now, that machine costs a fortune, and I guess those illegal modifications aren't cheap either, but as you can see above, a Reddit user used a 3D printer, a Raspberry Pi, and some other miscellaneous electronics and parts to make their own. It's an incredibly cool project, and it would make you the god-king of your local poker game, but I suspect it's going to be hard to convince your friends that they should use your homemade card shuffler when the next game night rolls around. Printing extra Scrabble pieces If you really need to get the last word in Some people take Scrabble far too seriously, and although this wonderful 3D model set of Scrabble tiles by jjpowelly are meant to let you replace lost tiles without buying a whole new box, clearly unscrupulous players could print out extra tiles and secrete them up a sleeve to gain an advantage. If you look closely at any of these tiles, it should be apparent that they are 3D-printed, but if you only slip in one or two letters, I bet you could get away with it. If you're playing with all 3D-printed tiles anyway, well, all bets are off, I guess. Printing your own tabletop miniatures is a gray area What would the emperor do? In the world of tabletop gaming, 3D printing has been rather controversial. This isn't about gaining an unfair advantage in the actual gameplay (which isn't how something like Warhammer works anyway) but more about copyright and intellectual property. With resin 3D printers and even modern FDM printers, you can create high-quality miniatures and then paint them. The tabletop community and the companies who sell official models to sustain themselves have had to reckon with this, and official games now have rules on what pieces may be 3D-printed, or how much of a given model is allowed to be 3D-printed. In the end, if you're using 3D printing as a way to avoid paying for (admittedly expensive) official models, there's certainly an ethical dimension to that. For no other reason than the hobby itself might disappear if this technology puts its custodians out of business. Follow your own conscience I can't stop you from printing whatever you want, and if you're just making stuff for your own personal amusement, there's no harm in it. However, with great power comes great responsibility. And owning a 3D printer gives you more than enough power to act in a fair and just manner.

item.title: My favorite kitchen upgrade proves that a real smart home is more than plugs and bulbs
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek Score: 2.27
Putting sensors all over the home and connecting them to Home Assistant is fun, I know, but it isn't for everyone — not yet. Thankfully, there are smart home upgrades that don't require any apps. I may have replaced every light switch in my home with a smart one, but my favorite smart home upgrade doesn't connect to my Homey Pro at all, and it's an improvement my entire family likes as much as I do. It's time to buy an instant hot water dispenser Our electric kettle has now entered the donate pile I didn't grow up with an electric kettle. Instead, my family boiled water in a saucepan on the stove whenever we wanted to make tea. Discovering an electric kettle as an adult felt like black magic. As a tea lover, this was a giant leap forward. When Waterdrop reached out to me about their M6CG instant hot and cold countertop water dispenser, it felt like a similar leap forward. After just one use, I knew I wasn't going back. My wife and two kids all had the same reaction. We haven't reached for our electric kettle since. In fact, we're giving it away. A countertop instant hot water dispenser doesn't take any time to boil, so I can stop taking shade from my European colleagues whose 240V kettles boil water much faster than is possible in America. A countertop hot water dispenser instead functions more like a tankless water heater, heating water as it comes out to get it to the right temperature. Since we're talking about a small stream of water, they can function off a regular 120V wall outlet with no extra electrical work required. Just place your cup under the dispenser, press the button, and watch hot water instantly dispense. Set water to the temperature you need Some units also turn off automatically after pouring the right amount I'm an avid tea drinker, but that doesn't mean I've taken the time to do it right. Before now, I turned my kettle on, waited for it to come to a full boil, and then poured water into my mug. It didn't matter whether I was drinking black tea, green tea, or herbal tea — I steeped them all at over 200 degrees. If you're cringing at this, I get it. It's no wonder I never liked green tea before. Waterdrop's dispenser has a control panel on the front that lets me set the temperature I need. I can't set exact temperatures and must instead settle for increments of around 20 degrees, but that's a huge step up from what I had before. The Waterdrop M6CG also wants to know how much water to dispense. With an 8oz mug, this is awesome. We can place a mug under the dispenser, tap a few buttons, and walk away to set a timer. When we return, the tea has already steeped in the time that it would take an electric kettle to come to a boil. This process may not be automated, but you can add it to the list of ways a smarter home can help you get up in the morning. An under-sink model greatly helps with washing dishes If you're a homeowner, I can't recommend this upgrade highly enough While I like the M6CH enough that I wouldn't go back to an electric kettle, it is far from a perfect product. This particular model is huge — too tall to fit under most of my kitchen cabinets. It's also very heavy, being about as unwieldy to move as a Ninja Slushi XL. This is particularly frustrating if you have to move it in order to lift the water tank in the back, which you'll need to do every other day as you dump out the old water and add in the new. This dispenser is also limited to dispensing 4oz, 8oz, 16oz, or 20oz of water, but not the 12oz that many of my family's mugs hold. Thankfully, I was also sent the Waterdrop K6 under-sink model, which places an instant hot water dispenser next to your kitchen faucet. I was able to install it myself with a couple of hours of work. The resulting dispenser doesn't take up space on my counter and never has to be manually refilled or emptied. While it can't automatically stop dispensing the way the countertop model can, it dispenses water much faster, so there is hardly any need. While I still use this model for tea, it's just as useful for washing dishes. It can't fill an entire sink with water, but the K6 can instantly pour hot water directly into a bowl or pan. I've found this to make easy work of even the most soiled of dishes, and this upgrade has drastically reduced how much scrubbing is required. As a parent who spends hours of my day at the kitchen sink, I love this upgrade dearly. It's not the only smart home upgrade I've made in my kitchen, but it's easily my favorite. Don't limit your smart home imagination to IoT devices Neither of these hot water dispensers is internet-connected, and there is no Matter logo on the side of the box. Yet being able to get hot water instantly, and at a precise temperature, is exactly the sort of awesomeness I envision a smart home being able to deliver. While homeowners have the most flexibility to install the best models, with countertop options available, renters don't have to miss out. That's good, because purified drinking water is the perfect upgrade to pair with that water tracker you 3D printed.

item.title: Android makes switching password managers much easier
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.50
What you need to know - You can now move passwords and passkeys directly between supported apps on Android without exporting sensitive data to an unencrypted file. - Your new password manager hands the process to Android, which detects compatible managers installed on your phone and coordinates the transfer. - Once authorized, Android moves the credentials between apps without requiring manual file handling. Android has always made it a pain to switch password managers. Moving passwords usually involved exporting your data into an unencrypted text file, and passkeys were pretty much stuck in place. Android is tackling both of those issues with a new transfer experience that makes moving your credentials much more secure and simple. In a blog post, Google said the new system lets you transfer passwords and passkeys directly between password managers, without first having to download a file. That eliminates one of the biggest security hassles of the old process, which was that sensitive credentials were sitting unprotected on your device for a while. Furthermore, passkeys weren’t transferable, so you had to manually recreate them across websites and apps. The process is built to be mostly out of your way. Start in your new password manager and select the option to import or copy credentials from another provider. The app then hands the job to Android, which knows which compatible password managers you have already installed on your phone and shows you where the data can come from. You are then sent back to the password manager you already use to select, review, and approve the transfer. Once approved, the passwords and passkeys move between the apps in just a few seconds. The feature is already available with Google Password Manager, 1Password, Bitwarden Password Manager, and Dashlane. Dashlane notes that CXP is compatible with devices running Android 10 or newer with the latest Play Services update. Bitwarden needs Android 14+ with Play services 26.21+. It is not merely a matter of convenience. Passkeys are more secure than passwords and resistant to phishing. Adoption has been stalled in part due to user concerns around vendor lock-in. CXP removes that barrier. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Bitwarden says the creation of passkeys peaked this summer at over 500% compared to early 2024, with nearly half of all passkeys created in the past three months alone. Google says more partners are on the way. If you’ve been waiting to change password managers because of the hassle, that excuse just went out the window. Jay Bonggolto always keeps a nose for news. item.title: Rokid wants anyone to build AI agents for its smart glasses
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 5.08
What you need to know - Rokid's AIUI Studio is a browser-based platform that lets anyone build spatial AI apps for Rokid Glasses, with no coding experience or dev kit required. - Developers can describe an idea, while the AI-native workflow helps turn it into a working app. - The built-in smart glasses simulator lets developers create and test projects before getting physical hardware involved. Rokid is making it easier to build apps for its AI glasses, and you won't need a coding background or even to own a pair of the glasses. The company has launched AIUI Studio globally at IFA Berlin 2026, giving developers a browser-based platform for creating and publishing spatial AI applications. Much of the development process takes place via an AI-native workflow in AIUI Studio. You can say what you want to build in plain language, and the platform can take that idea and build an app without the traditional coding skills. It also offers a simulation of Rokid’s smart glasses, enabling developers to work on their projects without having to purchase the hardware. There’s still a reason to get the real hardware involved eventually, though. Rokid’s developer documentation advises testing agents in its Interactive Inview simulator before performing a final check on the actual glasses. For developers who want to have more control, Rokid pairs its AIUI Skills Library framework with AIUI Code assistance. The company says this helps creators make better use of the glasses’ hardware while also optimizing apps for less latency, less memory use, and less power consumption. The move is the latest as Rokid’s developer ecosystem continues to grow. The company says it now has some 35,000 registered developers and more than 500 agents available through its Agent Store. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android AIUI Studio is now available worldwide. If Rokid can take advantage of that growing developer base to create a steady stream of useful agents, its glasses might just become a platform that people actively build around. item.title: Ray-Ban Meta glasses update makes them more useful on the go
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.91
What you need to know - Meta AI glasses v28 update adds pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, expanded language support, and camera anti-tampering improvements. - With hands-free walking directions, you can ask Meta to navigate to nearby destinations, with driving directions sent to your phone for farther trips. - Spatial Audio makes listening richer and adds a more immersive layer to music and podcasts on supported Ray-Ban Meta glasses. Meta has been steadily expanding what its AI glasses can do, and the latest v28 update adds several practical upgrades, including pedestrian navigation, Spatial Audio, and broader language support. Perhaps the headline addition is pedestrian navigation. You can now ask the smart glasses to guide you on foot to nearby destinations using voice commands such as “Hey Meta, navigate to Times Square.” If you’re farther away, the glasses can send driving directions to your phone. There’s also a new way to begin navigation from your phone: Find a destination in your mapping app, tap Share, and select Meta AI, and navigation will start on your connected glasses. The update also broadens where walking directions work. Meta says it now offers walking directions in the U.S., Puerto Rico, Canada, and some cities across the world. Audio gets an upgrade as well. Now, Spatial Audio can make a more immersive version of the stereo sound you’re already getting, whether that’s music or a podcast. You can find this option in Settings > Audio > Spatial. It works with Ray-Ban Meta Gen 2 Optics and the Meta Glasses collection. Meta is also adding Mandarin Chinese (zh_CN) support across Device Controls, calls and messaging, media capture and music controls, Meta AI, and MMAI. Finally, v28 has ongoing anti-tampering improvements to protect the cameras on the glasses. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android Earlier firmware releases introduced features like Conversation Focus, which uses the microphones in the glasses to help users hear nearby voices better, and deeper Spotify integration. Similarly, on Reddit, the response is pragmatic, with users mostly praising the glasses for hands-free photos, calls, podcasts, and open-ear audio, while battery life and Meta AI’s limitations remain common complaints. item.title: Arm's upcoming GPU for Android claims it can deliver 'desktop-class' graphics—I hope it's true
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 4.41
What you need to know - Arm revealed the work put into empowering its new Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU, which is said to bring "desktop-class" graphics to phones. - Arm states it's leaning on an AI-native Mali GPU with a Neural Accelerator and more to handle demanding graphics, while maintaining smooth frame rates for mobile gamers. - Qualcomm also teased its upcoming Adreno GPU for the next Snapdragon chips, stating it will also lean on AI to help with graphics rendering and frame rate generation. Arm is highlighting what mobile users can expect from its next GPU. It states everything it's worked to implement is due to growing user demands for "richer visuals" and better frame rates. Arm revealed the Mali G2-Ultra NX GPU in a newsroom post this week. According to its data, Arm says mobile users want a few things: "They want richer visuals, smoother frame rates, and increasingly immersive experiences." However, there are certain challenges it reportedly needs to overcome to help consumers (and developers, too). The Mali G2-Ultra NX is purportedly the answer to everyone's problems. Arm states it built the GPU for "neural graphics." This is an AI-native Mali GPU—its first-ever—which brings the Neural Accelerator into shader cores. This reportedly aids better teamwork between the graphics and computing workloads. What's more, performance is said to increase. Arm states its Neural Accelerator helps the GPU "handle increasingly demanding scenes more efficiently." This would give developers creating more pleasing visuals more room without the cost of reduced frame rates. Arm's third-generation ray tracing technology will also assist the graphics department. The Mali G2-Ultra NX support for this ray tracing software will facilitate advancements in shadows, complex lighting, reflections, and more. At a hardware level, Arm states devices with Opacity Micromaps support can produce "richer foliage, more detailed fabrics, layered surfaces, and more." Better graphics are nothing without smooth frame rates. Arm says "architectural improvements" in the GPU can support longer gaming sessions at "up to" 120FPS. AI comes to the aid of mobile graphics? We've been hearing about AI's involvement with mobile phone graphics since earlier this month. Qualcomm highlighted its Adreno "Neural Fusion" GPU, stating that it will lean on AI to upgrade mobile gaming graphics. The chip reportedly utilizes AI-driven rendering tech. This new tech will put better gaming resolution and frame generation in the graphics pipeline. Console-like graphics were a major detail for Qualcomm in that announcement. The company claims its new chip, coupled with AI, will reduce the work the chip needs to do to produce the graphics mobile users have been asking for. All of this is en route to the Dual 8 Elites from Qualcomm during the Snapdragon Summit from September 22-24. item.title: Samsung is shutting down a couple of apps; vows to return new and improved
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.76
What you need to know - Samsung is alerting users about its preparations to shut down the Quick Measure and AR Doodle apps on December 31, 2026. - While Samsung acknowledges "inconveniences" from this, it states that it's "committed" to returning these apps "with improved services" in the future. - In July, Samsung officially axed its Messages app, which has been replaced by the Google Messages app. Samsung is preparing to shut down two apps, and it's delivering warnings to users in preparation for what's to come. Very early this morning (Sept 7), Tarun Vats on X noticed new warnings from Samsung about two apps that are being phased out. Samsung says that it will shut down the Quick Measure app on December 31, 2026. It adds, "After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it's already downloaded, but be aware that some features may not function properly." The Quick Measure app currently works with Google's Wear OS. However, after this termination date from Samsung, it says app support will no longer be provided for new Wear OS versions. Quick Measure isn't the only app getting the boot. Users replying to Vats' thread on X mentioned Samsung's AR Doodle is also getting axed come December 31. A similar warning to users was given for AR Doodle. The date remains the same; however, it swaps Wear OS for regular OS, as this app likely relies on Android/One UI updates. While Samsung recognizes that shutting down an app can cause "inconveniences," the news isn't all bad. Samsung says, "We are committed to returning with improved services in the future." It's not clear if Quick Measure and AR Doodle will return upgraded, new, and improved. Or if we'll see brand-new variations that change these older systems. Another app got shutdown this summer Not going to lie, I had to dig pretty far back to even find anything about Quick Measure. Not sure how many people are going to miss the feature, but I'm there are some out there. It's interesting, considering everything the Samsung Health app can do today. If Samsung is committed to returning in some revamped form, I wonder if these features would find new lives inside existing, supported apps, rather than standalone gigs. If you're confused about "Quick Measure," we wouldn't blame you. Our earliest coverage dates back to 2021, when Samsung rolled out new features for its S Health app (yeah... S Health). That update coincided with the company's Gear Fit 2 launch. Quick Measure let users check their heart rate without launching the full app. Our coverage read, "Simply activate Quick Measure, and you'll now be able to place a finger on the heart rate sensor and wait for a reading." We've come a long way with heart rate tracking and the like related to cardiovascular health. Anyway, the last app shutdown from Samsung was its Messages app in July. Google Messages was reported to be the company's official replacement for users to text. However, consumers with Android 11 and under "are unaffected, and emergency calls still work after the shutdown." item.title: Samsung might've started racing ahead to Android XR glasses with a color display
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.54
What you need to know - Rumors claim Samsung is developing a new pair of smart glasses, and has tapped Samsung Display for an in-lens color display. - The glasses would allegedly focus on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and more" on an extremely thin panel. - Samsung has its Intelligent Eyewear, which is supposedly coming out this fall, but those are mostly voice-focused with Google's Gemini and a camera. Samsung has barely dipped a toe into the world of smart glasses, and there's already a rumor that it wants to go bigger next time. This report from The Elec (Korean) claims Samsung might've started developing smart glasses with a color display (via 9to5Google). The publication cites its "industry sources" in saying Samsung has tapped Samsung Display to "create microdisplays" for a future pair of AI smart glasses. These rumors claim Samsung has a lot on its plate to prepare this product. Specifically, the post claims Samsung has a "technical challenge" to overcome: its FOV (field of view). The company is purportedly chasing a wide FOV for these glasses to accommodate the information users would see. What's more, Samsung is leaning on its Display side to create "ultra-small panels" of ~0.2 inches or smaller for the lenses. Samsung is allegedly focusing on displaying "text, notifications, icons, and navigation arrows" (machine-translated). It's still incredibly early to know for sure how Samsung's first color display smart glasses will arrive. However, the publication suggests the glasses could see a launch in the second half of 2027 or "early" in 2028. Got lenses? Samsung's getting serious. I don't think its Intelligent Eyewear are a bad start, though. It's starting simple. Useful, even. Everything is based on your voice. You still have a camera to take photos, and Gemini is there to help with hands-free assistance. To put a color display—a proper screen—would definitely take things up a notch. To me, I think this rumor is probably a little more eye-catching. We can't help but think about the Ray-Ban Display glasses from Meta. In fact, that's probably the kind of competition Samsung wants to get itself involved in. These glasses also feature the neural band. It makes it easier to control the display and content on your lenses with hand gestures. There's plenty of time still to see how Samsung manages this. Right now, we have (kind of) Samsung's "Intelligent Eyewear." These glasses are in partnership with Google, alongside designs from Warby Parker and Gentle Monster. These are Samsung's first smart glasses, but they lean more on the user's voice. Users can communicate with Gemini for navigation, order pickups, and photos. The glasses feature a camera and a microphone to get all of this done. Google reiterated its Samsung partnership during this summer's Unpacked. These glasses aren't out yet. During the original announcement this past spring, Samsung said we shouldn't expect to see them until "later this fall." item.title: RIP Pixel Tablet: Google has officially pulled the plug
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 3.20
What you need to know - Google has officially removed the Pixel Tablet from its online store after listing it as out of stock. - The Pixel Tablet has also disappeared from major retailers including Amazon and Best Buy. - Google reportedly canceled plans for second- and third-generation Pixel Tablets due to sales and profitability concerns. - Existing Pixel Tablet owners will continue receiving software updates until mid-2028 despite the lineup's end. The Pixel Tablet is finally dead. Like, properly dead dead. Google launched the Pixel Tablet back in 2023 as a hybrid device that could work as both a traditional Android tablet and a smart home display when placed on its charging dock. At $499, the Pixel Tablet offered a pretty interesting combination on paper, but reactions to the device were mixed after launch. Google reportedly had plans for a second-generation Pixel Tablet in 2025 and even a third-generation model in 2027. But amid poor sales and profitability concerns, the company reportedly pulled the plug on those plans back in 2024. Despite that, the original Pixel Tablet remained available through the Google Store and retailers for quite some time. Until now. As spotted by Jetstream, Google has officially removed the Pixel Tablet from the Google Store. The tablet was listed as "out of stock" until a few days ago, but the product page has now been removed altogether, effectively confirming that Google is done selling the device. The Pixel Tablet has also disappeared from retailers, including Amazon and Best Buy. That means there's now no official way to buy a new Pixel Tablet. You may still be able to find remaining stock through smaller online retailers or pick one up from a reseller, but Google's own inventory is officially gone. The good news for existing Pixel Tablet owners is that software support isn't ending anytime soon. Google is expected to continue supporting the device with updates until mid-2028. But unless Google decides to resurrect its tablet ambitions again, there won't be another Pixel Tablet waiting to replace it. The Pixel Tablet was an interesting idea. Having one device that could work as both an Android tablet and a smart home display made plenty of sense, especially inside Google's ecosystem. Unfortunately, the idea never really took off. Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android So, RIP Pixel Tablet. This time, it looks like it's actually over. item.title: This new slim phone puts a 6,000mAh battery in a seriously thin frame
item.description:
Source: Latest from Android Central Score: 2.28
What you need to know - The TECNO Camon Slim 5G is here, and it's just 6.39mm thick while packing a hefty 6,000mAh battery. - It features a curved "swan-neck" profile and five distinct finishes, including photochromic technology on the Neo Mondrian variant and a swirling Starry Night gradient on Van Gogh Blue. - Despite its slim profile, it boasts MIL-STD-810 drop resistance, IP69K/IP69/IP68/IP66 water/dust ratings, and wet-hand touch functionality. TECNO appears to be pretty serious about the whole “slim phone” thing. Its latest phone, the Camon Slim 5G, is a mere 6.39mm thin but packs a 6,000mAh battery, a 50MP Sony camera, and a number of AI features into its compact body. The device also places a lot of emphasis on design. The Camon 50 series’ curved “swan-neck” profile is carried over from the Camon 50 series, but five finishes give the phone very different personalities: Burgundy Red, Neo Mondrian, Matisse Black, Van Gogh Blue, and Rebel Pink. Some of those finishes are very interesting. Neo Mondrian uses photochromic technology to show colorful geometric blocks on UV light, while Van Gogh Blue has a patterned gradient coating to create a swirling effect based on The Starry Night. item.title: Ukraine starts building a jet-powered drone with a range of over 1,000 kilometers
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.67
- Ukraine has started European production of its BARS jet-powered strike drone - The latest BARS configuration reportedly has a 1,000 kilometers range - BARS can now carry warheads weighing up to 60 kilograms Ukraine has begun production of its BARS jet-powered strike drone in Europe, and the latest version has a range of 1,000 kilometers. Production commenced in early September, intending to support higher output as developers continue to modify the drone for different mission needs. This is a joint effort between Ukraine and Germany, with the first completed drones expected to reach Ukraine's Defense Forces from October 10 2026. BARS enters European production with longer reach The arrangement followed an agreement signed July 8 by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius. Germany is financing the first production stage, while completed systems are intended for use by Ukraine's armed forces. Engine availability remains a key limitation, since turbojet deliveries currently determine how quickly additional aircraft can leave production. The BARS jet-powered strike drone can travel above 700 kilometers per hour while carrying a substantial warhead. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! However, with several modifications and upgrades, the newest configuration can reportedly travel 1,000 kilometers. Its maximum warhead weight has also increased substantially, rising from 22.5 kilograms on earlier models to 60 kilograms. Its design allows developers to alter fuel storage and payload capacity based on the distance required for a particular mission. Longer missions can use additional internal space for fuel, while shorter flights can devote more room to carrying additional weight. Developers keep changing the drone and its guidance BARS has reportedly gone through more than 40 design changes and upgrades since the prototype was developed. The platform is divided into DeepStrike, MiddleStrike and FrontStrike configurations, covering different mission ranges and operational requirements. The developer says artificial intelligence now contributes to several stages of the program, including engineering work and the drone's final guidance system. “We use the tools that AI technologies provide us today, and we do not shy away from them at any level—from development and solving engineering problems to implementing machine vision in our target-guidance systems,” said the BARS developer. During the final part of its flight, the operator can continue controlling the drone or transfer control to optical guidance. This expansion of BARS production is a strategically sound move for Ukraine because German financing and supply chain ease pressure on Kyiv's defense budget. Producing BARS in Europe also shields manufacturing from Russian strikes that have repeatedly targeted Ukrainian defense facilities. For Germany, this partnership signals a deepening commitment to Ukraine's long-term defense industrial base rather than merely short-term arms transfers. It strengthens bilateral ties and proves that European backing can translate into real, sustained battlefield capability. Such a longer-range, heavier-payload drone with AI-assisted guidance raises Moscow's defensive costs by threatening targets deeper behind the front line. This forces Russian air defenses to stretch across a wider geography, while the joint-production model may set a template for future allied co-production deals. item.title: FBI launches investigation after 153 million drivers licenses apparently leaked on Russian cybercrime forum
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.61
- 153 million US driving licences have been leaked on a Russian cybercrime platform - Among those apaprently discovered in the stolen data is US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth - The FBI is now investigating the leak, which has been traced to an identity verification company A data leak of 153 million US drivers licenses is said to have been shared on a Russian cybercrime forum, with US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth among those leaked prompting an FBI investigation. Security researcher Brian Krebs identified the leak – which included his own data – as originating from a hack of an identity verification service. Louisiana-based IDScan provided ID verification for various well-known companies, including FedEx and Hertz car hire. The data was shared on a Russian forum called Exploit, a long-established online community of cybercriminals. Following news of the leak, the identity theft service “Nexus” has apparently scrubbed its existence from the Dark Web. Driving licenses and more It wasn’t just US driving licenses that were found in the archive of recently-collected personal data. Krebs’ investigation found that Nexus claimed other types of data, and found a further 1.1 million driving licenses from Canada. Other identity documentation alleged to be in the leak include 10 million identification cards, three million travel documents and international IDs, and 579,000 medical cards. The data was available to browse, notes Krebs, with Nexus providing details: “Records are available to preview before purchase with pertinent information redacted. Customer photos are displayed if available.” The leak has a personal dimension for Krebs. Not only was his driving license in the collection, so was that of his mother. It has proved to be a useful coincidence, one that has enabled the security and privacy researcher to establish how the data was sourced by Nexus. Both licenses were used for a car hire, which Krebs traced to Hertz. Others affected by the leak had also used the service, which has used New Orleans-based IDscan for identity verification. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The company, which claims to perform 21 million verifications a month, is yet to issue a statement on the matter. Its marketing and operations leader, Jillian Kossman, told the journalist: “At this point I’m not able to share any additional information, but the updates you have provided have been welcome, and helpful to our team’s investigation.” Where is the data? Krebs reports that he was alerted to the data on August 31, 2026, little over a week ago. Regular checking noted that the data was still being added to, increasing by “nearly 400,000” records prior to publishing his investigation on September 1. Since then, however, it seems that Nexus has vanished, along with the data. But how widely was the data downloaded before that happened? While the FBI investigates, it falls on the American and Canadian public to be extra vigilant and wary of identity fraud. item.title: The US Navy is powering drone ships with Rolls-Royce engines which can drive for up to 30 days without human intervention
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.46
- The US Navy approved Rolls Royce engines for autonomous surface vessels - The certified engines can support missions lasting up to 30 days - Series 4000 engines completed two separate 720-hour durability trials The US Navy has approved Rolls-Royce marine engines for unmanned vessels capable of operating for periods reaching 30 days without crews onboard. The certification covers mtu Series 4000 and Series 2000 engines following tests examining their suitability for extended autonomous naval missions. The approval comes as the Navy expands its use of unmanned surface vessels for missions where keeping sailors away from danger remains important. Rolls Royce engines clear tests for autonomous vessels The Series 4000 completed two separate 720-hour durability assessments before receiving approval for propulsion and onboard electricity generation duties. That engine can deliver as much as 4,300 kilowatts for propulsion while providing up to 3,000 kilowatts through its electrical generation system. The smaller Series 2000 gained approval after component checks and operational trials, allowing it to provide propulsion output reaching 1,939 kilowatts. Both engine families can now support Navy vessels designed for lengthy missions without requiring people aboard for routine maintenance or repairs. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! The certification followed requirements established through the National Defense Authorization Act, which sets conditions governing equipment used within autonomous military platforms. The Navy has already begun deploying unmanned boats, including Sea Hunter vessels fitted with twin mtu 12V 2000 engines supplied by Rolls Royce. That deployment gives the newly approved engines a direct connection with the Navy's growing fleet of vessels designed for remote operations. The company says its propulsion systems have supported naval operations for decades, while newer autonomous missions create different demands for endurance. “For decades, mtu engines have been trusted to provide reliable, mission ready power for our crews at sea,” said Scott Hanson, vice president of governmental sales at Rolls Royce Power Systems North America. Longer missions create new demands for naval engines The ability to keep a vessel operating for 30 days without onboard personnel changes how the Navy can use unmanned surface craft. Such vessels can remain at sea for extended periods while avoiding the accommodation, support, and immediate safety requirements associated with crewed naval platforms. Rolls-Royce said the certification gives the Navy additional options as unmanned vessels become part of its wider fleet plans. The company also supplies propulsion equipment for several unmanned aircraft, including the MQ 4C Triton and MQ 25A Stingray platforms. Its portfolio also includes engines used by the United States Air Force's RQ 4 Global Hawk unmanned aircraft. The latest approval therefore extends an existing relationship between Rolls Royce and American military programmes into autonomous maritime operations. The certification does not mean every unmanned vessel using these engines will automatically achieve 30-day endurance during actual missions. Actual operating duration can vary according to vessel design, speed, weather, payload, fuel capacity, mission demands, and maintenance requirements. For the Navy, the immediate significance lies in having certified propulsion options for vessels expected to spend longer periods operating without crews. As more unmanned boats enter service, engine reliability will remain important because failures far from support facilities can impede mission success. item.title: Rebellion says Alien Deathstorm is a 'dynamically generated' survival horror game with sandbox elements and 'not another corridor shooter' — 'It's a rare beast'
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 5.24
- Alien Deathstorm producer Martin Willingham says the game is "not another corridor shooter" - Head of design Ben Fisher says it's a "dynamically generated" survival horror game - The Rebellion developers say it's a 360-degree sandbox experience Rebellion Developments has said players can't expect its upcoming first-person survival horror game, Alien Deathstorm, to be another linear corridor shooter, calling it a "rare beast." Alien Deathstorm was revealed earlier this year by the developers behind the Sniper Elite series and Atomfall and is described as a "visceral first-person action horror experience, where second-to-second survival hinges on responding to a monstrous, constantly shifting threat on a storm-blasted off-world colony." TechRadar Gaming recently went hands-on with the game at Gamescom and then later caught up with some Rebellion developers, who talked more about it at length, including the concept and design influences, replayability, and player freedom. While Alien Deathstorm may look like your run-of-the-mill survival shooter with typical survival horror features, the team considers it a "dynamic" experience with sandbox elements where the player's actions can affect unscripted enemy encounters. Producer Martin Willingham said this means, "the horror, the tension, can happen at any time in different ways between playthroughs and between difficulty camps as well. "For me, that's one of the most exciting parts of the game because in horror games the experience is typically kind of very, very choreographed because it has to be to build up that anticipation set of those jump scares. But it means you can only play it once." He continued, saying the team values replayability and sandbox freedom, which means "we had to do something dynamic," and "building the encounters around the player and the player's activities means it's a different experience." Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more. Ben Fisher, head of design, called the game "dynamically generated," where levels are played sequentially, and each has its own sandbox, adding that "It's a rare beast." "It's not another corridor shooter," Willingham added later. "You're in that sandbox. It's 360 degrees. The action could be coming from anywhere, rather than just at the end of that corridor." Alien Deathstorm doesn't have a release date yet, but you'll be able to play it in Spring 2027 on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, Series S, and PC. item.title: Palantir and Anduril awarded a $192 million US Army contract to build TITAN data-gathering system
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 4.92
- The US Army has moved TITAN from prototypes into production - Palantir received $127 million under the latest TITAN contract award - Anduril secured $65 million for TITAN hardware and integration work The US Army has shifted its Tactical Intelligence Targeting Access Node (TITAN) program from prototype status into full production this week. Palantir Technologies and Anduril Industries together received a combined $192 million award covering the next production phase. The Army first selected Palantir back in 2024 to serve as lead contractor for developing this next-generation targeting system for ground forces. Contract splits work between two defense firms TITAN was built to streamline how soldiers collect and process data when locating and striking distant targets on the battlefield. Palantir secured $127 million of the total award and will oversee TITAN's production alongside several supporting partners in the effort. Those partners include L3 Harris Technologies, Sierra Nevada Corporation, Strategic Technology Consulting and World Wide Technology, each contributing specialized capabilities to the program. Anduril received the remaining $65 million and will build the hardened, vehicle-mounted units required for field deployment. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! Anduril's portion also covers integrating power systems and thermal management components, so TITAN functions reliably in harsh operating conditions. The program includes two distinct configurations built for different vehicle platforms and mission requirements across Army units. An advanced version will mount on tactical trucks and can pull data directly from orbital sensor networks overhead. A simpler basic version is intended for the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle, giving smaller units similar targeting capability. Under the current award, contractors must deliver four advanced units and four basic units within eighteen months. Production ramp builds on existing prototype fleet These newly ordered units will supplement nine prototype systems the Army already operates and uses in current exercises. Army officials have indicated they plan to issue further production contracts for TITAN sometime during fiscal year 2027. The move from prototype to production status marks a milestone for a program meant to modernize how ground troops gather targeting information. TITAN forms a central piece of the Army's broader push to overhaul aging ground systems across its combat formations. By linking space-based sensors with vehicle-mounted terminals, the system aims to shorten the time between spotting a target and engaging it. Whether that translates into a meaningfully faster targeting cycle in real combat conditions remains to be tested at scale. The involvement of five separate companies alongside Palantir and Anduril suggests the Army is spreading technical risk across multiple vendors. That approach could either strengthen the program's resilience or complicate coordination as production accelerates toward the 2027 follow-on orders. For now, the contract signals steady progress rather than a dramatic leap forward for the broader modernization effort. The scale of future procurement will depend on Army requirements, funding decisions, and how the systems perform during operational evaluation. - AMD is putting data center-class AI hardware inside a desktop workstation - The Halo Station combines 96 CPU cores with four powerful AI accelerators - Up to 2.6TB of memory gives enormous AI models more local headroom AMD's Threadripper Halo Station could become one of the most extreme desktop workstations ever built for demanding artificial intelligence workloads. The device combines a 96-core processor with AMD Instinct accelerators and a huge memory pool designed for large local models. Unlike conventional workstations, AMD is building this system around data center-class computing hardware inside a single deskside machine. AMD packs data center hardware into a desktop At the heart of the Halo Station is the Ryzen Threadripper PRO 9995WX, based on AMD's Zen 5 architecture and carrying 192 threads. AMD lists up to 2TB of RDIMM system memory, while the accelerator side can add as much as 576GB of HBM3e memory. The accelerator configuration can use four Instinct MI350P units, with each device carrying 144GB of HBM3e memory and 4TB/s bandwidth. That design gives the machine a far larger high-speed memory pool than typical professional desktops built around a single graphics card. AMD compares the system with Nvidia's DGX Station, whose GB300 platform offers 748GB of coherent memory across its CPU and GPU resources. The comparison shows why AMD is focusing heavily on memory capacity, rather than treating processor core count as the main selling point. A machine with this much memory can keep larger models and datasets close to the compute hardware instead of constantly shifting them elsewhere. Halo Station is built for local AI work AMD says the workstation is intended for researchers, model developers, engineers, creators, and organizations that need intensive workloads handled locally. Its main role is running, training, and fine-tuning large AI models that would normally require access to expensive remote computing infrastructure. The system can handle frontier-class models while supporting hundreds of AI agents operating within the same local environment. That capability makes it useful for development tasks where repeated cloud transfers create delays, added costs, or data control concerns. AMD also says the design allows sensitive data and intellectual property to remain on premises instead of moving through external cloud services. The company unveiled a prototype at IFA 2026, with commercial availability planned for 2027. AMD senior vice president Jack Huynh described the device as “the most powerful workstation in the world,” emphasizing its unusual computing scale. Rack-mounted systems can cost far more than desktop workstations, so the Halo Station is not necessarily the world's most expensive computer. item.title: Boeing is turning the MQ-25 Stingray drone into an electronic warfare heavyweight
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News Score: 3.94
- Boeing receives $12.68 million investment to update the MQ-25's RF blanker, encrypted storage, and mission computer security, running through November 2029 - The change is a recent one: the Navy's April 2026 acquisition report lists refueling as the MQ-25's primary mission and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) as secondary, with no electronic warfare requirement and only two key performance parameters - An RF blanker is electromagnetic compatibility hardware that stops an aircraft's own transmitters from deafening its receivers, allowing it to conduct EW more effectively A single line buried in a recent US Department of War contract announcement is being read across multiple channels as the Navy's first carrier-based drone acquiring multiple electronic warfare upgrades. The details, however, seem to focus on the defensive side of the spectrum and include a Radio Frequency Blanker Unit and an updated Encrypted Mass Storage System carrying an embedded Data Transfer System. The modification also provides an option for deficiency analysis and corrections, supporting security assessments of the aircraft's Mission Management System Computer. Why do these upgrades matter? The most important upgrade for the MQ-25 Stingray, arguably, is its RF Blanker. An RF blanker is electromagnetic compatibility equipment. When an aircraft carries several transmitters and sensitive receivers within a few meters of each other, a transmitter firing at full power can deafen or damage a nearby receiver operating in an overlapping band. A blanker fixes that by taking a blanking request from each transmitter and issuing a suppression pulse to the affected receivers for the duration of the transmission, as GE Aerospace describes. For a drone that could also house sophisticated EW capabilities in the future, this is essentially a prerequisite. The Navy's Modernized Selected Acquisition Report dated April 21, 2026, offers a relatively narrow scope for the drone for now; however, it states that the MQ-25 conducts aerial refueling as its primary mission and provides Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance capability as a secondary mission. It is fairly possible that the upgrades are purely defensive, to prevent rogue players from accessing the drone or knocking it offline with relative ease. In its current capacity, the MQ-25 serves as an unmanned aerial refueling drone for the US Navy, offering capabilities including the ability to carry roughly 14,000 to 16,000 pounds of fuel at a combat radius of 500 nautical miles. Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! This could change even as the US continues hardening its EW offerings and prepares for potential hostile actors to have the same capabilities it currently harbors. For now, the $12 million invested in what is a $19 billion program is essentially a rounding error at the end of the day. This sudden investment may signal more to come: Boeing has already pitched a land-based MQ-25 variant with external pylons and marketing language about ISR, electronic warfare, and airborne early warning roles, though the aircraft has no customer yet.
