item.title: Healthcare AI’s next test is integration
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 4.43
Sponsored Provided byEnsemble The entrance of major AI companies into healthcare is a meaningful and welcome development, accelerating the technical foundation available to the industry. Their models are increasingly capable of processing long clinical records, interpreting complex terminology, comparing documentation against evidence and generating coherent summaries from large volumes of information. For clinicians, operators, and administrative teams who spend significant time searching through fragmented data, these advances are helping reduce cognitive burden and make high-value information easier to access. But healthcare leaders should not confuse model capability with operational capability. Healthcare’s administrative challenges are caused by fragmented information, fragmented workflows, and fragmented accountability, not a lack of information. The industry has spent decades investing in systems that capture activity: electronic health records, billing platforms, payer portals, scheduling systems, call center platforms, and analytics applications. Each system records something important. But few were designed to reason across the full chain of decisions that determines whether patients get timely access, clinicians have the right documentation and providers are reimbursed appropriately. This is the problem that AI must now confront. Revenue cycle is becoming one of healthcare AI’s proving grounds The revenue cycle is the process healthcare providers use to get paid for care — from scheduling and registration through coding, billing, payer follow-up, and payment collection. It is unusually suited to rigorous AI deployment because it combines high transaction volume, complex reasoning, structured and unstructured data, measurable outcomes, and significant operational variation. It also sits at the intersection of financial performance, patient access, and administrative workload. A single claim can be influenced by patient insurance information, clinical documentation, coding rules, payer-specific policies, prior authorization requirements, medical necessity criteria, and many other data sources and operational processes. A breakdown in any one of those areas can create downstream consequences weeks or months later. This is why generic automation has often fallen short. Traditional robotic process automation works well when workflows are stable and rules are predictable, but healthcare administration is neither. Payer requirements change. Documentation expectations evolve. Exceptions are common and often material. Large language models improve part of the equation, extracting meaning from narrative text, summarizing records and supporting reasoning over complex documentation. But when used alone, they inherit important limitations. They may produce plausible outputs without sufficient traceability. They may lack awareness of local workflow constraints. They may miss payer-specific history or context that determines whether an action is likely to change an outcome. Why foundation models will become necessary but insufficient The major AI firms are solving real technical problems for healthcare. Better context windows make it easier to process longitudinal records. Stronger reasoning improves the interpretation of complex clinical scenarios. Better multimodal capabilities may eventually help connect text, imaging, structured data, and clinical signals in more useful ways. Safer model behavior and healthcare-specific tuning will continue to improve adoption. These capabilities will make healthcare work faster, more consistent and easier to navigate. But they will not, on their own, solve deep-rooted administrative complexity. Much of healthcare’s operational knowledge does not live in general medical literature, coding manuals, or public payer guidance. It lives in the accumulated experience of what actually happens after decisions are made. For example: - Why does one appeal strategy outperform another? - Which documentation gaps are most likely to cause reimbursement delay? - How does a specific payer respond to a particular clinical argument? These insights are behavioral, operational, and longitudinal. They emerge from years of transactions, outcomes, exceptions, and human judgment. As foundation models become more capable, access to baseline healthcare knowledge will become less differentiating. Most leading systems will be able to interpret ICD-10 codes, recognize medical terminology, summarize payer policies, and reason over public clinical criteria. The durable advantage will come from how organizations combine that model intelligence with proprietary operational data, structured knowledge, workflow context, and governance. The technical shift: From automation to orchestration Agentic orchestration turns foundation model understanding into coordinated action — intelligence that can follow work across systems, apply the right rules, adapt when something changes, and keep learning from what happens next. A prior authorization workflow, for example, may require retrieving clinical documentation through fast healthcare interoperability resources (FHIR) APIs, mapping patient history to payer criteria, identifying missing evidence, generating a submission packet, routing exceptions to a specialist, monitoring payer response, adjusting patient care pathways, and learning from the outcome. This type of workflow requires coordination. It also requires guardrails: regulatory requirements, privacy standards, clinical policies, coding rules, payer criteria, and organizational risk thresholds. One promising approach is hybrid architecture that combines LLMs with structured knowledge bases, symbolic logic, reinforcement learning, and deterministic validation layers. At Ensemble, this is the design principle behind EIQ, our revenue cycle intelligence engine. EIQ brings together operational activity, clinical documentation, payer behavior, and reimbursement outcomes into a continuously learning intelligence layer that’s integrated with the hospital’s electronic health record (EHR). It supplements the system of record with a system of intelligence, designed to connect information and surface actions most likely to improve outcomes. EIQ uses a neuro-symbolic approach that combines LLMs and custom small language models with rules-based reasoning. That architecture is built on one of the most robust datasets in healthcare, informed by more than a decade of award-winning operational performance, transaction history, payer behavior, and operator decision-making. The language models help interpret information and generate human-readable outputs. The symbolic layer represents policies, rules, payer requirements, and workflow constraints so the system can apply guardrails, make reasoning steps more traceable and recommend actions that fit the specific operational context. What the next decade will reward The contribution of major AI firms to healthcare will be significant. Their models will become faster, safer, more capable, and more accessible. But the next decade of healthcare AI will be defined by integration, not model capability alone. The organizations that create the most value will be those that connect models to governed data, operational workflows, domain expertise, human oversight, and measurable outcomes. They will understand that healthcare intelligence cannot live in a separate interface. It has to exist inside the decisions that shape access, documentation reimbursement, and patient experience. This content was produced by Ensemble. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. And it’s looking for influencers to give it a try. Montana’s plan to become an experimental medical hub just pushed forward The state’s effort to expand the “right to try” is making headway, and the first drugs are about to be reviewed. There’s a lot of hype around perimenopause. Don’t buy it. Discussions of the life stage are often clouded by misinformation. item.title: This road map could help us decide whether to deploy solar geoengineering
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 3.24
A San Francisco nonprofit has published a detailed road map of the experiments, studies, and infrastructure that it says would be needed to make informed decisions about the use of solar geoengineering, MIT Technology Review can reveal. Scientists have now spent half a century exploring the possibility that we could counteract climate change by releasing reflective particles into the stratosphere, mimicking the cooling effects of volcanic eruptions. But even after at least hundreds of studies on the concept, known as stratospheric aerosol injection (SAI), big gaps remain in the scientific understanding of how well it would work and what else it might do—and there has been no systematic plan for clearing up that uncertainty. Reflective, a research organization that funds studies on solar geoengineering, has today attempted to fill that gap with the release of its SAI Research Roadmap. “Our mission is to equip the world with the data and tools required for informed decision-making about sunlight reflection fast enough to matter,” says Dakota Gruener, the organization’s cofounder and chief executive. “Our sense is the world may need to make very consequential decisions on timelines far shorter than our research system is prepared for.” The hope is the exercise will guide scientific efforts and encourage philanthropies or government agencies to fund high-priority work and “responsibly accelerate research,” says Gruener. If all the work is done in a coordinated way, it would take about a decade and cost around $370 million—and if it’s not, it would require roughly 20 years and nearly $1.4 billion, the report estimates. While Gruener stresses that Reflective doesn’t advocate using this form of solar geoengineering, the report does make the case for conducting outdoor experiments, which would release successively larger amounts of sulfur dioxide (or materials that would convert into it) in the stratosphere to observe what happens. That is a controversial standpoint. Since 2002, hundreds of academics have signed an open letter calling for a ban on outdoor experiments and an "international non-use agreement," arguing that such a powerful technology could never be governed in a globally equitable way. And some signatories argue that more studies can never address one of the biggest questions about using solar geoengineering: Who gets to do it. “The first-order questions, from my perspective, are not technical,” Aarti Gupta, co-initiator of the non-use initiative and professor of global environmental governance at Wageningen University in the Netherlands, told me in a recent on-stage interview. “The core question is: Who would control a planet-altering technology like stratospheric aerosol injection? Who would develop it, and who would deploy it, and to what end? To serve what purposes, and whose purposes? Those questions are very fundamental, because this planet-altering technology will have winners and losers.” ‘Fast enough to matter’ Since Gruener incorporated Reflective in late 2023, the nonprofit has quickly become an important player in solar geoengineering research. It has now raised more than $20 million from a number of prominent charities and individuals, and it’s provided around $4 million to several dozen research groups. Reflective has also undertaken a handful of its own projects to promote research, including the development of an open-source solar geoengineering simulator and an online hub for collaborative research. Earlier this year, Reflective released its SAI Uncertainties database, which identified a long list of scientific unknowns and engineering obstacles that would need to be addressed before even a small-scale solar geoengineering effort could move ahead. (I wrote about the specific scenario and the unknowns in this earlier piece.) Some of the biggest uncertainties involve what gas or particles would make the most sense to use and what would happen once they were released in the dry stratosphere. It’s not clear, for example, whether they’d spread out in a way that maximizes the reflectivity—or clump together and quickly fall out into the troposphere, the lowest layer of Earth’s atmosphere. The road map builds upon the database, highlighting the path to addressing most of those questions. The road map The initial phase in Reflective’s road map, labeled “foundational knowledge,” includes additional computer simulation studies and lab experiments designed to shed light on the potential impacts on different regions, ecosystems, and phenomena, including ocean circulation patterns, ice sheets, and crop yields. The report also notes the need to begin developing more observational tools during this phase to improve understanding of the baseline conditions of the stratosphere—and, in turn, our ability to assess any effects from the eventual release of materials. This first stage would last two to three years and cost $30 million to $75 million, though some of the analysis and observational work would continue into subsequent phases. The next stage would include using modified aircraft to release 10 metric tons of sulfur dioxide into the stratosphere, four times over the course of two seasons. The full research stage could take four to eight years and cost $70 million to $150 million, the report says. The work during it may reduce uncertainty about the “cooling efficacy” of solar geoengineering, or how much the planet would cool per ton of sulfur released, by about 25%. The experiments during the next phase would step those levels up dramatically, releasing 25,000 tons of sulfur dioxide over the course of one season, at least once but possibly twice. That research stage, which includes other work as well, would last four to 11 years, run $270 million to $1.1 billion, and decrease efficacy uncertainty by around 66%, according to the road map. The final phase of research would be ongoing monitoring of full-scale solar geoengineering, if the world goes ahead with it. The goal would be to gather real-life data on the technology in action, update estimates of the effects in models, and spot any “unexpected or undesired consequences.” Gruener says that the road map is intended as a Version 1, meant to be “concrete enough for people to argue with.” But Reflective intends to update the plan as it receives additional reactions from researchers and other observers, and it will invite such feedback through a mechanism on the site. She also notes that there are firm “stage gates,” set up between the latter stages—in other words, research shouldn’t proceed to the next phase if the experiments suggest that the releases don’t have the hoped-for impact, show worrisome downsides, or fail to resolve crucial uncertainties. “Our road map has these gates precisely because there may be points where the answer is ‘You should stop,’” she says. Termination shock Most observers I spoke to about the report agree that these studies could reduce uncertainty about the effectiveness of solar geoengineering and our technical ability to carry it out. But highlighting the scientific importance of outdoor experiments won’t necessarily make them any easier to move ahead with. Several earlier proposals to carry out such experiments, including Harvard’s SCoPEx and the UK-based SPICE project, were ultimately halted amid opposition from environmentalists or policymakers. In addition, not everyone agrees that experiments at those scales will get us to the point where we’re capable of making an “informed decision.” Wil Burns, a research professor and legal scholar at American University and a signatory to the International Non-Use Agreement, fears that scientists won’t be able to understand the extent of the potential downsides, including impacts on the protective ozone layer and changes to regional precipitation patterns, until we’re carrying out full-fledged solar geoengineering. “The research would give you some answers,” he says. “I just don’t think it gives you answers that are that relevant. To get to those relevant answers, you have to deploy at scale—and I just don’t think that’s ever tenable.” That’s because, in his view, using the technology would violate principles of intergenerational equity: If the world continues emitting greenhouse gases, increased levels of solar geoengineering would merely mask the continued warming of the planet. Burns says that means future generations—people who had no say in its use—couldn’t turn it off without triggering a sudden surge of warming, known as termination shock. “What that would do, in my mind, is put a sword of Damocles over future generations,” he says. “So even if you could, quote-unquote, ‘prove it works,’ I don’t think from an intergenerational perspective it would ever be tenable.” (Some researchers, however, have argued that the risks of termination shock are less likely than often assumed—and that solar geoengineering could be slowly dialed down over time.) ‘The right approach’ Ilan Gur, the former CEO of the Advanced Research and Invention Agency (ARIA), the UK research department that funded 21 geoengineering research projects last year, applauds Reflective’s road map. “Whether you’re a scientist or a policymaker or just a concerned citizen, our goal should be as quickly and efficiently as possible to answer the biggest questions scientifically that would tell us [whether] this is an approach that might work or that would never work,” he says. “We should all want to spend the effort and money to buy down that uncertainty, so my view is 100% the approach that Reflective is taking is the right one.” Sebastian Eastham, an associate professor in sustainable aviation at Imperial College London who is leading an ARIA-funded research project exploring another approach to engineered cooling, agrees that the outdoor experiments described in the Reflective road map can’t resolve all the unknowns. But he says the map helps begin a conversation about how to make decisions concerning the use of a tool with potential benefits and risks, in the face of escalating climate dangers. “Every hard decision that has ever been taken has been in the context of unresolved uncertainty,” he says. “That’s just the nature of things.” Eastham adds that it’s become essential to move beyond computer simulations to address some of the key questions, arguing that appropriately designed and executed outdoor experiments can teach us so much more than millions of hours of computational processing time “that it almost becomes irresponsible to say, ‘Well, there cannot be ever any experiment.’” The risk is “that we spin our wheels running the same computational simulations over and over and over again,” he says. That could prevent researchers from learning essential things about the effectiveness or the dangers of stratospheric aerosol injection. Weighing the risks Gruener says the risks that solar geoengineering could exacerbate inequality need to be considered, but notes that unchecked warming also threatens to disproportionately harm developing regions. She also acknowledges that outdoor experiments won’t fully address the scientific unknowns but stresses that they can answer a lot—and carry little environmental risk. She notes that 10 tons of sulfur dioxide is less than 2% of the amount that the global aviation industry releases into the atmosphere each day. “Some people will be uncomfortable with any discussion of any outdoor experiment, but if we want decisions made on good science … then these are questions that an experiment will be necessary to address,” Gruener says. She fears that the rising dangers of climate change will put growing pressure on nations and other actors to move forward with solar geoengineering, even if no one has done the necessary research to reduce scientific uncertainty and sort out the technical challenges. “We don’t think the alternative is decisions not happening at all,” she says. “We think the alternative is decisions being made in a panic or on lack of evidence.” Deep Dive Climate change and energy Why heat pumps are still so hot in the US A key tax credit in the US ended, but heat pump sales are still going strong. item.title: Powering AI is an architecture problem
item.description:
Source: MIT Technology Review Score: 2.12
Sponsored Provided byON.energy On July 22, 2026, a transmission line fault in Ashburn, Virginia—the heart of the world's largest data center cluster—knocked more than 3 gigawatts of load off the grid in seconds. And it wasn't the first time. Two years earlier, a single failed surge arrester dropped roughly 60 Virginia facilities and 1,500 megawatts at once. No one could anticipate so much uniform load responding to grid faults the same way, at the same time. The AI power debate is mostly about generation: more turbines, more solar, more transmission. The grid needs more electrons. But the outages in Virginia weren't supply failures; they were architecture failures. And a giant wave of interconnections is arriving on that same architecture, putting grid reliability at risk. It's a problem nobody wants to own. Asking more from the grid The grid was built around predictable loads: steel mills, refineries, and houses at dinnertime. Different load sizes, same process—drawing power smoothly, misbehaving occasionally, and recovering gracefully. But AI data centers don't behave that way. An AI campus can swing 70% of its load in milliseconds during a training run, then trip offline just as fast at the first sign of trouble upstream to protect billions in compute. Each is rational alone. Together, at gigawatt scale, they're a problem the grid has never solved—and the next wave of data center campuses is planned at exactly that scale. Where the old stack breaks The standard data center power stack hasn't changed in decades. Medium-voltage power arrives, transformers step it down, low-voltage uninterruptible power supply (UPS) units condition it, and it reaches the racks. Push that design to AI scale, and it cracks in three places. First, the UPS sits deep inside the building, close to the racks. But its batteries are an undersized spare tire, designed to handle an outage for a few minutes, not to absorb load swings this fast and volatile around the clock. Second, the UPS spends most of its life in bypass. Legacy converters waste enough power that operators run in eco-mode: A static switch feeds the racks directly from the grid and nothing filters in either direction. The compute's swings go out raw, and grid transients—sub-millisecond events that can damage or take down equipment—come in too fast for any switch to catch. Third, the protection logic was written when "large load" meant 50 megawatts. This protection logic can't see the grid it is now a part of, so when trouble hits upstream, it does exactly the wrong thing: it drops out. In the 2024 Virginia event, most of the lost load traced to protection schemes that count voltage dips and disconnect on the third one—as designed, at the worst moment. This isn't sloppy engineering. It's careful engineering the load has outgrown. Moving into the path The fix is three moves, made together. Move it up—from 480 volts to medium voltage (13.8 kilovolts and higher), the voltage large sites draw from the grid. Move it out—from the data hall to modular enclosures near the substation so the building holds only compute and the cooling that keeps it alive. Move it into the path—instead of a battery that watches and reacts, a system every electron runs through, all the time. There's nothing to detect and nothing to switch because nothing was ever routed around it. On paper, three straightforward upgrades. In practice, they rewrite every line item downstream. Making the change When thousands of GPUs spin up together, the system absorbs the swing and hands the grid a flat load profile. When a disturbance hits, the equipment behind it never notices. A difficult neighbor becomes a predictable one. And when the utility needs help, it becomes a useful one. Interconnection changes, too. The utility certifies one medium-voltage box instead of untangling every transformer, UPS, chiller, pump, and switchgear lineup behind it. Engineers swap chip generations without a fresh interconnection study. Months come off the permitting timeline. Inside the fence, UPS rooms become compute or cooling space. Density per construction dollar climbs. And the economics flip. Equipment that runs at medium voltage, sits outside, and stores its own energy can qualify for tax credits, and earn revenue in grid programs like peak shaving and demand response. Backup power stops being insurance and starts paying for itself. The architecture test In early 2026, we tested a full-scale system at the National Laboratory of the Rockies, a U.S. Department of Energy facility and the only place in the Western Hemisphere that can replicate real grid faults and AI-scale load swings concurrently in the same loop. We hit it from both directions: real AI load profiles hit the compute side at full medium voltage. Grid faults hit the utility side, including a full zero-voltage event. The compute side didn't flinch. Neither did the grid side. It cleared the large-load voltage ride-through requirements from the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), the grid operator, with room to spare. Those rules exist because operators no longer take facilities this size on faith, and more are coming. Most of the industry treats them as hurdles. A medium-voltage, inline system clears them out of the box. Compliance isn't an added feature. It's what the architecture does. The new layer Much of what looks like a grid problem in the AI buildout sits inside the fence, in equipment sized for a load that no longer exists. Move the right pieces up, out, and into the path, and a grid liability becomes a grid asset. Density goes up. Permitting time comes down. Backup power earns its keep. The engineering works—and the next wave of AI factories is being built on it. The industry hasn't named this layer yet. We call it the medium-voltage AI UPS. The name matters less than the choice: those factories can arrive as a strain on the grid or as strength for it. We already know how to build the second kind. This content was produced by ON.energy. It was not written by MIT Technology Review’s editorial staff. Deep Dive Artificial intelligence A fundamental flaw leaves LLMs strikingly vulnerable to attack It makes it easy to trick them into doing things they shouldn’t, such as telling you how to sabotage an aircraft’s navigation system. AI is more likely than humans to form biases when hiring AI doesn’t just learn stereotypes from its training. It can cook up new ones, too. item.title: Company Linked to Theft of 153M Driver's Licenses Confirms Possible Breach
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 6.04
IDScan.net admits it may have suffered a breach, after a hacker appeared to steal over 153 million driver’s licenses from the vendor’s ID verification system. Louisiana-based IDScan hasn’t responded to requests for comment about the situation. But cybersecurity journalist Brian Krebs, who first reported that a mysterious site on the dark web was selling access to millions of US and Canadian driver’s licenses, also discovered that the company quietly posted a “Notification of Data Security Incident” on its website. The notice, dated Sept. 4, says IDScan is investigating a possible breach. “While the investigation is ongoing, IDScan.net has determined that an unauthorized third party may have accessed and/or copied certain customer information stored within their accounts on the IDScan.net cloud,” it says. “The types of information contained within the affected data may include full names and driver’s license or other government-issued identification numbers.” IDScan offers identity card and passport verification services to clients, including the rental car company Hertz, delivery provider FedEx, and video game retailer GameStop. The alleged breach suggests the company was storing IDs from numerous consumers, who were likely unaware. If confirmed, the breach could be one of the worst in recent history, exposing millions of people to identity theft. For now, IDScan says it’s providing affected users with free credit monitoring and identity protection services and is urging them to be vigilant against phishing and fraud. Interestingly, IDScan’s breach notification page doesn’t appear in major search results because the company added code to the site to prevent web crawlers from indexing it. In the meantime, some consumers are already suing IDScan. Court records appear to show that over a dozen class-action lawsuits have been filed in the US against the company, up from four a week ago. The FBI also told PCMag it’s been investigating the potential breach. The dark web site that was selling the 153 million driver’s licenses appears to have been removed, but the hackers could easily spin up a new site or sell the information to other cybercriminals through private channels. item.title: Apple May Be Prepping Ads for Visual Intelligence on the iPhone
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.54
You may soon get ads when using Visual Intelligence on your iPhone. Code spotted in the latest iOS 27 build suggests Apple is preparing an option for sponsored results within its AI-powered camera recognition tools. Visual Intelligence uses Apple Intelligence to let you learn about your surroundings, analyze items, find information about locations, or ask what’s happening on your phone’s screen. MacRumors' Aaron Perris noticed iOS 27 code that “indicates that Apple may be working on supporting ads from search providers" within the tool. “This would not be Apple selling the ads, but more so allowing sponsored images like you see in Amazon or Google listings," he says. Perris didn’t clarify which element of the code he found that suggests ads are coming, or how far through development it appears to be. If Apple is developing this, however, you may get a sponsored link to buy through an online retailer when you point your camera at an item you find in a rival brick-and-mortar store. Perris also notes how it’s unclear whether Apple would take a revenue cut from ads shown within Visual Intelligence. Apple takes a percentage of all digital sales made through its App Store, so it may choose to do something similar here. Apple hasn't made any announcements, but it has increased advertising features on its products in recent years, including a rollout of ads in Apple Maps in August. The ads appear in the Suggested Places feature when you use the search bar, labeled with a blue box icon. item.title: Asus Receives Exemption to US's Foreign-Made Wi-Fi Router Ban
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.40
Taiwanese PC maker Asus has received a temporary exemption to the US ban on foreign-made Wi-Fi routers after the Defense Department determined that its products do not pose a national security risk, the Federal Communications Commission announced on Wednesday. An FCC exemption is good for 18 months, so Asus's "conditional approval" lasts until March 6, 2028. It applies to various Wi-Fi product lines, including the RT Router Series, ROG GT Series, ROG Strix GS Series, TUF Gaming Series, ExpertWiFi Series, ZenWiFi Mesh Series, 5G MiFi Series, repeaters, and wireless access points. The exemption is good news for Asus, as the Taiwanese vendor has begun preparing Wi-Fi 8 products ahead of the wireless technology’s official standardization. Last week, Asus announced the latest ROG Rapture GT-BN98 series had launched in Canada, with a global rollout slated for October. So far, Asus hasn’t responded to a request for comment. But when applying for an exemption, the company had to answer a long list of questions, including a “detailed, time-bound plan to establish or expand manufacturing in the United States for the router.” Currently, many routers imported to the US come from Vietnam, Mexico, Taiwan, the Philippines, and Thailand. Other router vendors that have received an exemption include Netgear, Amazon’s Eero, SpaceX’s Starlink, and Taiwanese brands Zyxel, Arcadyan Technology, and Asus subsidiary Askey Computer. But so far, the US has yet to grant an exemption to the major Wi-Fi router maker TP-Link, which has long been fighting accusations over its ties to China. The US enacted the ban—which only applies to new products—over concerns that foreign-made routers introduce "supply chain vulnerabilities" that hackers and cyberspies can exploit. However, TP-Link has been stressing that it’s a US company after relocating its headquarters to Irvine, California, and splitting off from the Chinese business. In April, TP-Link told the FCC it plans to invest “hundreds of millions of dollars” to bring its manufacturing from Vietnam to the US while previewing its plan to apply for an exemption from the ban. “Conditional Approval will enable TP-Link to complete those investments,” it wrote. item.title: Want a New iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone Duo? Here's How Much They Cost With Apple Upgrade
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.38
Apple announced during its 'Surprise and Shine' event that the iPhone 18 Pro will launch on September 18, with preorders opening on Saturday, September 12. Its first foldable, the iPhone Duo, will launch one month later on October 23, with preorder starting on October 16. If you can't wait to get your hands on either of Apple's latest premium flagships but can't afford to buy them outright, you have options. You can trade in your old device to shave some money off of your bill, finance with your carrier, or lease a device through Apple's newly launched Upgrade program. Here's how much the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone Duo will cost through Apple Upgrade, and whether or not this leasing option makes sense for you. How Much Is the iPhone 18 Pro With Apple Upgrade? The iPhone 18 Pro will start at a retail price of $1,199 in the US. If you want to lease the iPhone 18 Pro through Apple Upgrade, prices will start at $34.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $49.99 per month for a 24-month lease. The iPhone Duo will retail for between $1,999 and $3,199. Apple Upgrade plans for the iPhone Duo will start at $57.99 per month for a 24-month lease and $82.99 for a 12-month lease. How Does Apple Upgrade Work? In partnership with "buy now, pay later" (BNPL) platform Klarna, Apple Upgrade is a new leasing program that launched on July 28, which lets you pay a monthly fee for select iPhones and Apple Watches for 24 months and MacBooks and iPads for 36 months. You'll then have the option to return the device, pay off the balance and keep it, or upgrade to a new device. Eligibility will be based on a credit check. For an iPhone, it'll need to be connected to AT&T, T-Mobile, or Verizon when you enroll. This new service replaces Apple's iPhone Upgrade program. If you're currently a member of the iPhone Upgrade Program, your loan agreement with Citizens One remains active, and you’ll continue making your monthly payments until your 24-month term is complete, when "the iPhone will be yours to keep." Does Apple Upgrade Charge Interest or Fees? Neither Apple nor Klarna mentions any interest payments. Apple's current iPhone Upgrade Program is a zero-interest installment loan, and so was Apple Pay Later, which the company ditched in 2024. Apple says there are no fees on a monthly lease payment, but notes that you could incur a damage fee at the end of your lease term if you don't take care of the device. There are also fees if you upgrade or terminate a lease early. Plus, if you don't decide what to do at the end of your lease, Klarna will start an "automatic extension period" for up to 6 months. "During this extension, your monthly payment may increase because promotional credits (such as trade-in credits) only apply to the original lease term. If you still make no decision by the end of the extension, Klarna will charge a one-time payment, otherwise known as the Purchase Option Fee, to pay off the device. You will be notified 1 month in advance if your next payment will be the final payment." There were reports that Apple would restrict access to certain apps if payments were late, but sources tell PCMag that's not the case. "If a payment cannot be collected, Klarna will retry," Klarna says. "If that also fails, Klarna will attempt to charge a backup payment method on file. There are no late fees for this program. However, missed payments can eventually be sent to debt collection after multiple failed attempts, and missed payments may be reflected in your credit report." Should You Use Apple Upgrade to Lease a New iPhone or Mac? There are some scenarios where leasing an Apple product makes sense. Maybe you need a MacBook for grad school, but don't plan to keep it after you graduate. Or, perhaps you're already upgrading to the newest iPhone every year, and leasing will save you money. But even if the math works in your favor, make sure you understand all of the risks before you sign up. Which Products Can You Lease Through Apple Upgrade? While Apple Upgrade is available for most newer Apple devices, some older and budget versions are not available. You cannot use Apple Upgrade for the iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, Apple Watch SE, MacBook Neo, Mac mini, iPad (A16), or Studio Display. You can currently lease the following phones, MacBooks, iPads, and Apple Watches with Apple Upgrade: iPhones: - iPhone Duo - iPhone 18 Pro - iPhone Air - iPhone 17 - iPhone 17 e Macs: - MacBook Air - MacBook Pro - iMac - Mac Studio iPads: - iPad Pro - iPad Air - iPad Mini Apple Watches: - Apple Watch Series 12 - Apple Watch Ultra 4 - Apple Watch Hermès Series 12 - Apple Watch Hermès Ultra 4 How Much Does It Cost to Lease Other Apple Products? The main draw of Apple Upgrade is its low prices. Here are the starting prices by Apple device: - iPad - $11.99 per month - iPhone - $17.99 per month - Apple Watch - $11.99 per month - MacBook - $24.99 per month These are just starting prices and will vary by product (and possibly your credit score). Leasing an iPhone 17, which costs $899 to buy, starts at $25.99 per month to lease for 24 months and $36.99 to lease for 12 months. However, Apple says you can trade in your old device to lower your lease payments. For comparison, Apple's now-defunct iPhone Upgrade plan charges $42.41 per month for an iPhone 17 with 256GB of storage over a 24-month term. What's the Catch? We're glad you asked. There are a few big risks you should understand before you sign up for Apple Upgrade. Apple Upgrade Does Not Include AppleCare+ Apple Upgrade will not include AppleCare+, which protects your device against certain accidental damage. You'll have to add and pay for AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage yourself within 60 days of your lease starting. Without that protection included, you're on the hook for any damage. "You may incur damage fees if the device is...not returned in the condition required by the lease," Apple notes. If you don't have AppleCare+ Theft and Loss coverage, and the device is lost or stolen, you'll have to pay an early termination fee or the purchase option fee. If you do nothing, you'll continue to be charged the monthly lease fee. You May Get Trapped in a Cycle of Monthly Payments Much like streaming services require you to pay every month to continue to access your favorite movies, TV shows, and music, Apple Upgrade could keep you hooked on monthly payments for decades. Unlike financing an iPhone or MacBook, Apple Upgrade leases don't cover the full cost of the device, so when the end of your lease term arrives, you'll be on the hook for a large balloon payment, the Purchase Option Fee, if you want to buy your device outright. As an example, let's look at the cost of leasing the iPhone 18 Pro (which starts at $1,199). Lease prices start at $34.99, so if you leased this phone for 24 months, you'd have paid $839.76 after 24 months. So, you'd need to pay at least another $359.24 at one time in order to purchase and keep the phone. If you can't afford to make this large lump-sum payment on time, the easiest solution is to lease another device, essentially locking you into another couple of years of monthly payments. Suddenly, you're trapped in an endless cycle of monthly fees for a device you don't even own. About Our Experts As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert. I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week. My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth. My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work. Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well. As PCMag's managing editor of operations and evergreen content, I lead the operations, How To, and updates teams. I have 15+ years of experience writing and editing personal finance, small business, and financial software content. Prior to PCMag, I led the personal finance team at CNET. My work has also been published in the Chicago Tribune, NerdWallet, Investopedia, and BestReviews. Personal finance Project management software Tax software Accounting software Identity theft services Antivirus software A PC enthusiast for most of my life, I now work on a 14-inch MacBook Pro (M3) or 13-inch MacBook Air. You won't pry my Android from my hands, though! I have a Samsung S25 that has miraculously survived hundreds of accidental tumbles down my wood staircase. My first desktop was a hand-me-down Power Macintosh in the early '90s, where I spent hours trying not to get eaten by a grue in the game Zork. I'm an avid reader, and though I prefer physical books, I travel with my old Nook GlowLight 3 (yes, they still exist).

item.title: Polaris Freedom LT Cordless Robotic Cleaner Review: Basic But Effective Pool Maintenace
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.17
When I reviewed the Polaris Freedom Plus back in 2024, I gave it high marks for its cordless operation, underwater controls, and superb cleaning performance, but I thought its $1,649 price was a bit steep. The Polaris Freedom LT cleaner is a more affordable version of its sibling, and it too offers excellent cordless cleaning performance. However, you don’t get underwater control or dirty canister alerts, and it doesn’t expel water when you remove it from the pool. At $799, it’s still a solid value, but you’ll get more features, including an underwater remote and AI mapping, with our top pick for smart robotic pool cleaners, the $1,499 Dreame Z1 Pro, which can usually be found for less than the price of the Freedom LT. Designed for inground pools up to 50 feet long, the Freedom LT maintains the same two-tone blue-and-black color scheme as the Freedom Plus. It measures 9 by 15 by 17 inches (HWD) and weighs 16.5 pounds. It’s powered by a lithium-ion battery and uses two drive motors and a pair of bulldozer-style treads to navigate the floor, walls, and waterline of your pool. The battery is rated to last up to 3 hours per work cycle and requires around 4 hours to fully recharge. There's a gasketed power port on the back of the robot, and front and rear scrubbing brushes on the undercarriage. An optical sensor that aids with navigation sits on the front, along with a handle for removing the robot from the water. The top of the cleaner holds a water outlet, a control panel, and a transparent cover for the 4-liter filter basket. The main filter comes with a fine-mesh inner basket for capturing particles such as sand, pollen, and other grit. The main basket lifts out and can be easily emptied and cleaned with a hose without touching any debris. As with the Aiper Scuba V3 ($1,099.99), cleaning the fine filter can get messy, especially if you remove the mesh material from the basket for a thorough rinse. The control panel consists of a power button, an LED indicator, and four mode indicators. The power button turns the robot on and off, and cycles through the four cleaning modes: floor/walls, floor, walls, and waterline. Additionally, a multi-day mode is available in the app, allowing you to program the robot for up to four days of floor cleaning with a specific start time. Just leave the robot in the pool, and it will begin a 45-minute cleaning cycle at the specified time. Unlike the Dreame Z1 Pro, the Freedom LT does not offer AI mapping; instead, it lets you choose a cleaning path best suited to your pool’s shape. The S-Pattern is recommended for most pools, while the Standard pattern is best for pools with complex shapes. The Freedom LT uses a Bluetooth radio to pair with your phone and a Wi-Fi radio to connect to your network. As with every other pool robot, wireless connectivity is lost when the machine is underwater, so the only way to stop a cleaning cycle is to let it run its course or pull it out of the water with the hook. An underwater controller, something you get with the Freedom Plus and Dreame Z1 Pro, would be helpful here. When a work cycle is complete, or the battery is low, the cleaner will climb the wall and park itself along the side of the pool. It’ll stay there for 10 minutes before sinking to the bottom, where you can retrieve it using an included hook. Unlike the Freedom Plus, the Freedom LT doesn't expel water when removed from the pool, so it’s heavy to lift out of the water. The Freedom LT is the first Polaris cleaner to use the new Fluidra Pool mobile app for iOS and Android devices, whereas previous models work with the iAqualink app. The Fluidra app adds multi-day cleaning, lets you select cleaning patterns, and makes it easy to share access with service providers without revealing your personal credentials. To use the app, you must create a Site (home location) and assign each connected device to a Space (pool or spa). Individual logins for each Space let you manage multiple homes and devices from a single app. When you open the app, you’ll see a panel for the cleaner showing its name and current status (charging or offline). Tap the panel to open a screen showing the charging progress. Once the robot is unplugged, you can select a cleaning mode and a cleaning pattern in the Cleaning Mode panel. Here you can also create a multi-day schedule. Once the cleaner is programmed, simply drop it in the pool to begin the work cycle. As with the iAqualink app, Flurida does not offer work logs or dirty-canister alerts, but it will notify you when the cleaner completes a work cycle. The Freedom LT robot comes with a retrieval hook, a user guide, buoyancy foam to help it float to the surface, and an AC charger. Preparing the Freedom LT for first use is easy. I downloaded the app, created an account and a Site (home), and charged the robot for several hours until the LED glowed solid green. I tapped Add Equipment on the home screen and followed the instructions to scan the QR code located in the filter compartment. Once the app identified the cleaner, I entered my Wi-Fi credentials, created a Space (pool), and gave the robot a name to complete the installation. The Freedom LT performed well in testing. I have a ton of small berries from a neighbor’s tree that fall into my 16-by-32-foot gunite pool, and the LT had no trouble sucking them up along with a fair amount of filter sand. It averaged nearly 3 hours of battery life between charges and needed all of that to complete a full work cycle (floor, walls, waterline). In comparison, the Polaris Freedom Plus needed 2.5 hours, and the Dreame Z1 Pro finished the job in 2 hours. I had some trouble getting the multi-day cleaning feature to work at first, but after a firmware upgrade, it worked as intended. I used the app to set the cleaner to multi-day/floor-only cleaning with an S-pattern and programmed it for Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Friday at 5 p.m. The cleaner scrubbed the floor for 45 minutes, stopped, and started right back up at 5 p.m. the next day. It had just enough power to handle the four-day schedule before needing a recharge. As previously mentioned, cleaning the main filter basket with a hose was easy, but flushing out the fine filter took a bit more work. I had to remove the fine filter from its basket to clear all the sediment, which meant getting my hands dirty. On the plus side, I was happy to have the fine sediment out of the pool. Final Thoughts Polaris Freedom LT Cordless Robotic Cleaner - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.5 - Poor: Do not buy this product - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. The Polaris Freedom LT lets you spend less time cleaning your pool and more time enjoying it. At $799, it won’t break the bank, and it offers great cleaning performance, good battery life, and multi-day cleaning schedules. That said, you don’t get many extra features with this model. If you’re looking for a feature-rich pool robot that offers underwater control, work logs, and even better suction, our Editors’ Choice winner, the Dreame Z1 Pro, is your best bet, and you can find it for well under its list price via several online retailers. About Our Expert I’ve been working with computers for ages, starting with a multi-year stint in purchasing for a major IBM reseller in New York City before eventually landing at PCMag (back when it was still in print as PC Magazine). I spent more than 14 years on staff, most recently as the director of operations for PC Labs, before hitting the freelance circuit as a contributing editor.

item.title: Apple Satellite Features Will Be Free on iPhones for Another Year
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 5.12
The satellite features on supported iPhones will remain free for at least another year. "Apple is extending free access to satellite features for an additional year for existing iPhone 14, iPhone 15, and iPhone 16 users," the company wrote in the fine print of its iPhone 18 Pro announcement. That’s good news since the satellite features, including the Emergency SOS, were slated to expire in the coming weeks for affected iPhones. Satellite service keeps people connected in cellular dead zones, allowing them to send text messages via satellite. Emergency SOS has also helped emergency responders locate people stranded in remote areas. Apple describes the access as a “free trial,” so it could eventually charge for the satellite connectivity. But so far, it has instead extended free access, even though the satellite connectivity was initially advertised as a two-year free trial. Apple’s third-party partner, Globalstar, a satellite communications company, has powered the feature since late 2022, when it first arrived for the iPhone 14. Amazon is now in the process of acquiring Globalstar, including taking over Apple’s 20% stake in the company. Still, Amazon says it’ll continue supplying satellite services for iPhones and improving them through Globalstar. The iPhone satellite features have been limited to text messaging, location pinging, and emergency assistance. You also usually need to point your phone toward the right part of the sky to access it. Still, Amazon’s goal is to expand Globalstar’s technology with two next-generation satellite constellations and eventually offer voice and mobile data. But this also means the upgraded satellite tech might come at an extra cost for iPhone owners. In the coming years, consumers can also expect to see more satellite-to-phone service offerings. The two other major players, SpaceX and AST SpaceMobile, have ambitious plans to deliver cellular-focused broadband via orbiting satellites. About Our Expert I've been a journalist for over 15 years. I got my start as a schools and cities reporter in Kansas City and joined PCMag in 2017, where I cover satellite internet services, cybersecurity, PC hardware, and more. I'm currently based in San Francisco, but previously spent over five years in China, covering the country's technology sector. Since 2020, I've covered the launch and explosive growth of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, writing 600+ stories on availability and feature launches, but also the regulatory battles over the expansion of satellite constellations, fights with rival providers like AST SpaceMobile and Amazon, and the effort to expand into satellite-based mobile service. I've combed through FCC filings for the latest news and driven to remote corners of California to test Starlink's cellular service. I also cover cyber threats, from ransomware gangs to the emergence of AI-based malware. In 2024 and 2025, the FTC forced Avast to pay consumers $16.5 million for secretly harvesting and selling their personal information to third-party clients, as revealed in my joint investigation with Motherboard. I also cover the PC graphics card market. Pandemic-era shortages led me to camp out in front of a Best Buy to get an RTX 3000. I'm now following how the AI-driven memory shortage is impacting the entire consumer electronics market. item.title: Looking for the Limited-Edition Zelda Switch 2? We’re Tracking the Restocks

The Nintendo Switch 2 is already a pretty good-looking console, but Nintendo just gave it a limited-edition makeover. Preorders are open, and just like most limited-edition hardware from Nintendo, it sold out fast. But don’t give up just yet—we’re basically breaking the refresh button across the web to keep tabs on any future availability. It’s currently listed for $519.99, which is on par with the rest of the internet. Expectedly, there are no deals right now, and it’s sold out. But if it does become available here again, we suggest creating an account in advance to make sure you have all your ducks in a row before you buy. item.title: New AppleCare One Family Plan Covers Everyone's Devices
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.85
While all the attention at Apple’s Wednesday event was focused on the latest iPhones, Apple Watches, and AirPods, the company also briefly teased a new device protection plan that covers Apple devices owned by your family members. The AppleCare One Family plan drops on Sept. 14 for $49.99 per month and protects the Apple devices of up to six members in your Family Sharing group. With this plan, you don't have to purchase AppleCare+ for each device or family member, and it includes benefits such as unlimited repairs, 24/7 priority support from Apple experts, and theft and loss coverage for iPhones, iPads, and Apple Watches. Once you purchase the subscription, all eligible devices in your Family Sharing group, “including most devices less than four years old and in good working condition,” will be automatically added to the plan at no extra cost. Any new Apple device you purchase will also be included automatically. To remove devices you no longer use, go to Settings > General > AppleCare & Warranty. As noted by MacRumors, the Family plan builds on the AppleCare One Individual plan launched last year, which covers three devices for $19.99 per month and lets you add new devices for $5.99 per month each. With the Family plan, Apple’s fine print says you can make only six theft and loss claims per year, though there is no cap on accidental damage and warranty claims. The standalone AppleCare+ plan ($11 per month) offers two claims, and the AppleCare One Individual plan offers three. Apple announced the plan alongside the iPhone 18 Pro models, which start at $1,199, and the foldable iPhone Duo, which starts at $1,999. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

item.title: Amazon Is Using AI to Fix Terrible Dubbing on Its Streaming Shows
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.65
Dubbing can be useful for those who struggle to keep up with subtitles, but it's jarring when the actors' mouths don't line up with the audio. Amazon is looking to solve that problem on Prime Video by using AI and visual effects to synchronize the dub with the actors' dialogue. This lip-sync technology will appear first on Maxton Hall before expanding to other titles. It's already available on seasons one and two of the popular German series, and will also work on season three, which premieres on Dec. 9. "Syncing mouth movements to audio, it eliminates the disconnect that can occur with traditional dubbing," Amazon says. On Prime, searching Maxton Hall returned the original series and an option for "Maxton Hall - The World Between Us (with Lip Sync for English Dub)." The actors' mouths do appear to line up with the English words in that version. Filmmakers might not like it, but Amazon argues the lip-sync tech will make it easier for creators' stories "to reach an even broader and global audience, all done under creative oversight to ensure the integrity of their artistic vision is preserved." "AI and VFX technologies power the process behind the scenes, responsibly applied to deliver a better customer experience," it adds. Last year, Amazon announced a pilot program for AI-aided dubbing on licensed movies and series that would not have been dubbed otherwise. And YouTube added multi-lingual dubbing last year. About Our Expert Jon Martindale is a tech journalist from the UK, with 20 years of experience covering all manner of PC components and associated gadgets. He's written for a range of publications, including ExtremeTech, Digital Trends, Forbes, U.S. News & World Report, and Lifewire, among others. When not writing, he's a big board gamer and reader, with a particular habit of speed-reading through long manga sagas. Jon covers the latest PC components, as well as how-to guides on everything from how to take a screenshot to how to set up your cryptocurrency wallet. He particularly enjoys the battles between the top tech giants in CPUs and GPUs, and tries his best not to take sides. Jon's gaming PC is built around the iconic 7950X3D CPU, with a 7900XTX backing it up. That's all the power he needs to play lightweight indie and casual games, as well as more demanding sim titles like Kerbal Space Program. He uses a pair of Jabra Active 8 earbuds and a SteelSeries Arctis Pro wireless headset, and types all day on a Logitech G915 mechanical keyboard.

item.title: Apple AirPods 5 Are Somehow Cheaper Than AirPods 4
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.23
Apple's fifth-generation AirPods, announced Wednesday, come in two different versions, and the more advanced option is $20 cheaper than the equivalent AirPods 4 model. The cheapest option is $129, while a more advanced pair cost $149. Both versions are up for preorder later today, ahead of a Sept. 18 launch. Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) is now available across both standard AirPods models, and it's better than on the AirPods 4. Apple claims each offers up to 50% more noise reduction than its predecessor, calling it the "best ANC on the market" for an open-ear design. A new Adaptive Audio feature lets the headphones change ANC settings depending on what's happening around you. "Providing the best of both worlds, Adaptive Audio dynamically blends Transparency mode and ANC based on the conditions of a user’s environment," Apple says. Both models feature a redesign of the earbuds' internals, which Apple says includes a new multi-port acoustic architecture and its next-generation adaptive equalizer to deliver better audio than previous models. "This makes Personalized Spatial Audio more immersive and dynamic, so the user feels like they’re surrounded by whatever they are listening to," Apple says. How do the two models differ? The design is largely similar, but the more expensive option comes with enhanced controls built into the earbud's stem, similar to those on AirPods Pro. There's also an extra hour of battery life on the more expensive model, plus a wireless-charging-compatible case. The basic AirPods 5 feature four hours of listening time and 20 hours with their paired case. The more expensive option comes with five hours of listening and 22 hours with the wireless charging case. The earbuds also come with new tied-in features that pair with other Apple services, such as access to the upgraded AI-powered Siri in iOS 27 and Live Translation on iPhone. Apple's event today also introduced the iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and a foldable iPhone Duo. Apple didn't announce the long-rumored redesigned AirPods Pro, which are now expected to land next year. Rumors suggest Apple may include built-in cameras to monitor your surroundings for AI-powered features. How to Preorder AirPods 5 AirPods 5 are now available to preorder on Apple's website and will ship on Sept. 18. For more, check out our hands on with Apple's latest wireless earbuds. About Our Expert I’ve been a journalist for over a decade after getting my start in tech reporting back in 2013. I joined PCMag in 2025, where I cover the latest developments across the tech sphere, writing about the gadgets and services you use every day. Be sure to send me any tips you think PCMag would be interested in.

item.title: iPhone Price Hike Is Here: Older Models Now Up by $100, Even iPhone 16
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 4.12
If you were waiting to snag a deal on an older iPhone following the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro, you’re in for an unpleasant surprise. Apple has raised prices across its smartphone lineup by $100. The hikes were a long time coming, due to rising global memory and component costs. Former CEO Tim Cook dropped hints about “unavoidable” price hikes in mid-June, and the company immediately bumped prices on Macs, HomePods, iPads, and the Vision Pro. Old vs. New iPhone Prices The iPhone was spared from the first round of Apple hikes, but now they’ve been hit too. The newly launched iPhone 18 Pro models cost $100 more than their iPhone 17 Pro counterparts did at launch. Apple has now discontinued the older 17 Pro models and slapped $100 price hikes on all other existing models, including the regular iPhone 17, iPhone Air, and iPhone 17e. Here’s a look at the new and old prices of all the iPhones currently available for purchase at Apple, excluding the new foldable iPhone Duo ($1,999): - iPhone 18 Pro: Starts at $1,199 (up from $1,099 for iPhone 17 Pro) - iPhone 18 Pro Max: Starts at $1,299 (up from $1,199 for iPhone 17 Pro Max) - iPhone 17: Increased from $799 to $899 - iPhone 17e: Increased from $599 to $699 - iPhone Air: Increased from $999 to $1,099 - iPhone 16: Increased from $699 to $799 iPhone 17 Trade-In Values Alongside the hikes, Apple also released the trade-in values for the iPhone 17 series. For the iPhone 17 Pro and 17 Pro Max, you can get a maximum value of $885 and $785, respectively, while for the iPhone Air and iPhone 17, you can receive a maximum credit of $585. Apple Upgrade Leasing Program In case you’d like to reduce the up-front cost of your iPhone purchase without trading in your older device, you can check out the new Apple Upgrade leasing program as well. For example, leasing starts at $34.99 per month for 24 months on the iPhone 18 Pro. The 18 Pro Max starts at $37.99 per month. At the end of your plan, you can pay off the remaining balance and keep the device, leave the program and return the device, or upgrade to a newer model and start a new lease. iPhone 18 Pro and Duo Preorder and Release Dates Preorders for the iPhone 18 Pro models begin on Sept. 12, with shipments starting Sept. 18. Preorders for the iPhone Duo, meanwhile, begin on Oct. 16, with shipments starting Oct. 23. Stay tuned to PCMag’s coverage for detailed reviews of all of these devices, as well as the new Apple Watches and AirPods. About Our Expert Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. item.title: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 Looks Boring, But Its Battery Could Change Everything
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.75
CUPERTINO—The Apple Watch Series 12 blew me away at the company's launch event, leaving the new Apple Watch Ultra 4 in a tough spot. At $799, the Ultra 4 packs the same AI health insights, sharper sensors, and clever Audio Intelligence features as its $399 sibling—but it offers no exclusive smart features. Even its rugged titanium shell is unchanged from the Ultra 3, and Samsung's $700 Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 matches its dive and endurance credentials. Yet, there is one critical reason you shouldn't write off the Ultra 4 just yet: battery life. If history repeats itself, Apple's boosted battery claims could turn this repetitive upgrade into the longest-lasting major smartwatch ever made. The $799 Secret Weapon: Battery Specs Apple officially claims the Ultra 4 lasts up to 50 hours on a charge—up from 42 hours on the Ultra 3—thanks to a larger battery capacity and the more efficient S11 chip. For endurance athletes, Apple promises up to 84 hours in Low Power Mode and 45 hours of continuous GPS tracking, enough to power through a 100-mile ultramarathon. Here’s the catch: Apple almost always underpromises on battery. The Ultra 3 lasted 63 hours in my real-world testing, easily beating the company's claim, though it now falls short of Samsung's class-leading Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 (69.5 hours). Historically, when Apple bumps its official battery estimates, real-world performance gains are even larger. The Series 11's gain of 6 estimated hours added 7 real-world hours, while the Ultra 3's 6-hour official increase delivered 8 extra hours in daily use. If the Ultra 4 keeps that pace, real-world testing should hit 71 to 73 hours—dethroning Samsung to claim the top endurance spot. Early Outlook: Will Battery Life Save the Ultra 4? Even if it falls a hair short of setting a battery record, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 remains a formidable beast for extreme athletes, complete with a built-in dive computer and thermal resistance. But for everyone else, rugged specs and AI smarts simply aren't enough to justify a $400 markup over the seemingly stellar Series 12. The Ultra 4's entire value proposition rests on its battery life. If my real-world testing proves it can crack the 70-hour mark, Apple won't just have a solid upgrade—it'll hold the crown for the ultimate wearable endurance monster. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is available for preorder now and hits store shelves on Sept. 18. Be sure to check back soon for my full review. About Our Expert I’m PCMag’s senior writer covering smart home and wearable devices. I’ve been reporting on tech professionally for nearly a decade and have been obsessing about it for much longer than that. Prior to joining PCMag, I made educational videos for an electronics store called Abt Electronics in Illinois, and before that, I spent eight years covering the smart home market for CNET. I foster many flavors of nerdom in my personal life. I’m an avid board gamer and video gamer. I love fantasy football, which I view as a combination of role-playing games and sports. Plus, I can talk to you about craft beer for hours and am on a personal quest to have a flight of beer at each microbrewery in my home city of Chicago.

item.title: Why Apple's New iPhone 18 Pro Camera Still Needs Old-School Accessories
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.75
The iPhone 18 Pro has a cool new camera feature—variable aperture. It's an uncommon feature among smartphones, though not unheard of—the Huawei Pura 90 Pro Max from earlier this year has it too. Still, Apple needn't be first in everything, and since variable aperture lenses let you control how much light reaches the sensor, it's a useful feature for photography and video, though not the game-changer Apple would want you to believe. I've been reviewing cameras for more than 15 years, so I'm here to explain what variable aperture is, why you'd want it, and when you'll still need an add-on filter to reduce the amount of light entering the lens. The Basics: How Aperture Controls Light and Focus If you've only ever used a smartphone for photography, you're used to lenses that work at one and only one aperture, also called f-stop. In plain language, the aperture is a numerical value that indicates how much light a lens lets in and how much reaches a digital image sensor. Phones tend to use wide-aperture lenses that let in as much light as possible to capture good photos in tough light, and default to very short shutter speeds when taking photos or videos out in the sun. The main lens of the iPhone 17 Pro has an f/1.78 aperture, which is considered quite bright and ideal for taking photos in dimly lit environments. A variable aperture uses a set of blades that close down from the sides to block some of the incoming light. Getting less light into the system lets you more easily use longer shutter speeds to introduce some motion blur, and increases the depth of field, the fancy technical term for how much of a scene is in sharp focus. One bit of housekeeping: Apertures are expressed in fractions, so a smaller number means that more light is coming in. One Lens Only: The Fine Print The iPhone 18 Pro's main lens is rated for f/1.48, which means that when it's used with the aperture wide open, it is more sensitive to light than the 17 Pro's f/1.78 lens. But instead of being stuck wide open like the 17 Pro, the 18 Pro includes a six-blade diaphragm that closes down to f/1.8, f/2.8, or f/4.0. The iPhone 18 Pro adds a variable aperture to its main lens and redesigns its optics to gather more light. When used with the Camera app in automatic mode, the f-stop changes automatically based on the light. If you're taking photos in a dimly lit interior, it'll open to f/1.48 to let in as much light as possible. For beach days and sunny landscapes, the phone will narrow the diaphragm to reduce light. One note: The variable aperture is only included in the main 24mm wide-angle lens; it's not available on the ultra-wide (13mm) or telephoto (100mm) lenses. Those are unchanged from the iPhone 17 Pro. Unlocking Creative Exposure With Pro Controls You don't have to be stuck with automatic adjustments, however. Apple includes manual exposure settings, called Pro Controls, for both photography and video. These let you adjust various aspects of your exposure, including shutter speed, aperture, and white balance. Knowledgeable photographers can use manual settings, along with the variable aperture, to take more creative control over their pictures. There are two main reasons to use a small aperture. The first is depth of field. The iPhone 18 Pro's f/1.48 lens and Type 1/1.28 image sensor will be able to create some optical blur in the right situation. iPhone photographers are used to having to go into Portrait mode and use depth mapping to blur backgrounds, but given the physics behind the 18 Pro's camera system, it will achieve similar effects when the camera is positioned close to a subject and there is some distance between it and the background or foreground. I don't anticipate the iPhone 18 Pro giving you the soft-background bokeh look without portrait mode in many situations, even when the lens opens all the way to f/1.48. Once you put enough distance between the camera and the subject, everything is in focus from an optical standpoint. Using f/2.8 or f/4 may result in slightly sharper backgrounds, but not enough to notice on a 6-inch phone screen or in a social media post. Now, sunstars are another matter. Apple showed off the iPhone 18 Pro's ability to produce bright highlights with dramatic spikes. That's something that happens optically, not computationally. When light passes through an aperture, it takes on its shape, and narrower f-stops can make light particles scatter, an effect called diffraction. These diffraction spikes, commonly called sunstars in the photo world, can add drama to landscapes, cityscapes, and portraits. You won't see them in every photo, but they're easy to get if you catch a bright reflection off a piece of jewelry, bits of sunlight peeking through leaves, or sunlight on the surface of water. The Physical Limits: Why You Still Need an ND Filter The second reason to cut incoming light is to achieve long-exposure effects. I like to use a half-second shutter speed to smooth out flowing water for landscape photos that include streams and waterfalls, and I will go even longer for urban landscapes where I want to blur out pedestrians and cars. Videographers will try for what's called a 180-degree shutter angle to record motion with just a touch of blur, an effect that reads as more cinematic. To get this angle, you want to set your shutter speed to half of your frame rate—1/48-second for 24fps, 1/60-second for 30fps, and so on. For interiors, night scenes, and twilight, the f/1.48-4.0 aperture range will give you enough leeway for photos that intentionally blur motion and cinematic shutter angles, but it's likely to fall short under sunny skies. You'll still want to add a neutral density (ND) filter over the lens if you want to get some motion blur in bright light. I'm surprised that Apple didn't add computational tricks to boost its variable-aperture lens in these types of scenes. Granted, I haven't tested the phone yet, so it could simply be something Apple chose not to mention. Is Variable Aperture Worth the Hype? I plan to test the limits of the iPhone 18 Pro's camera for long exposures and other creative shots as soon as possible. On the surface, variable aperture feels like a nice addition, but it's far from a game-changer. If you're a casual snapper who just wants to capture moments with your phone, you won't ever have to think about the aperture. Apple's Camera app will decide where to set it, and you'll still want to use Portrait mode for a blurred background, because in most situations, optical blur won't deliver the bokeh look. Knowledgeable photographers and videographers will get more mileage from the f/1.48-4.0 adjustment range and should be savvy enough to recognize its limitations. If you're in this group, you'll still want to add a neutral density filter. And don't worry, you'll have the option if you want—as I write this, the iPhone has been public for all of 90 minutes, and I've already received an email from Moment, one of the biggest makers of photo and video accessories for smartphones, letting me know that it has an adjustable Variable ND filter ready for the iPhone 18 Pro. Apple's latest killer feature isn't enough to kill the accessory market. About Our Expert Images, and the devices that capture them, are my focus. I've covered cameras at PCMag for the past 15 years, which has given me a front row seat for the changeover from DSLRs to mirrorless cameras, the smartphone camera revolution, and the emergence of drones for aerial imaging. I have extensive experience with every major mirrorless and SLR system, and am also comfortable using point-and-shoot and action cameras. As a Part 107 Certified drone pilot, I’m licensed to fly unmanned aircraft systems (UAS) for commercial and editorial purposes, and am knowledgeable about federal rules and regulations regarding drones.

item.title: AirPods 5 vs. AirPods Pro 3: Are Apple's Pro Buds a Big Upgrade or a Big Mistake?
item.description:
Source: PCMag Score: 3.51
Table of Contents The first foldable iPhone might be the biggest news from Apple's September event, but that doesn't mean you should sleep on the new AirPods the company announced. The AirPods 5 come with active noise cancellation (ANC) as a standard feature, and they're waterproof—both qualities they share with the excellent AirPods Pro 3. The AirPods Pro 3 remain stunning in-canal earphones, but with the base model leveling up so drastically, it raises a massive question for your wallet: Is a single pair of AirPods Pro 3 actually worth two pairs of the new AirPods 5? Full Specs | Apple AirPods 5 | Apple AirPods Pro 3 | | |---|---|---| | Type | | | | Type | Open-style earbuds | In-Canal | | Wireless | | | | Wireless | | | | True Wireless | | | | True Wireless | | | | Connection Type | | | | Connection Type | Bluetooth | Bluetooth | | Water/Sweat-Resistant | | | | Water/Sweat-Resistant | | | | Active Noise Cancellation | | | | Active Noise Cancellation | | | Price: Pro Features at Half the Cost? At $129, the AirPods 5 rewrite the value equation by including active noise cancellation out of the box—eliminating the extra $50 tax Apple previously charged for ANC on non-Pro models. That slashes the price barrier in half compared with the $249 AirPods Pro 3, delivering flagship sound isolation without the premium markup. Winner: AirPods 5 Sound Quality: Open-Ear Fit vs. In-Canal Seal We can't evaluate how the AirPods 5 sound until we get them in for testing, but we can at least apply years of experience and the hard science of acoustics to compare them with the AirPods Pro 3. The AirPods 5, like all standard AirPods before them, are earbuds that rest against the ear canal but don't provide a seal as the in-canal AirPods Pro 3 do. There's a limit to how consistently earbuds can fit in the ear and how much deep bass they can produce without a seal, which can make a big difference in performance. To be fair, the AirPods 4 sound excellent even without a seal, but the AirPods Pro 3 are without a doubt superior. Apple claims the AirPods 5 have a revised internal acoustic design for better audio, but for clarity and power, you can't beat a physical plug that prevents frequencies from leaking into the open air. Winner: AirPods Pro 3 Noise Cancellation: Physics Always Wins As with sound quality, noise cancellation performance is something we have to test ourselves to be sure, but you can't get around the reality of acoustics. Because the AirPods 5 don't form a seal against the ear canal, noise can leak in, no matter how sophisticated the ANC processing is. Apple's claims are also pretty clear, by the numbers.
