item.title: Electric air taxis get the green light for test flights in Texas
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.85
A new federal program to test the feasibility of electric, hybrid-electric, and autonomous aircraft kicks off today in Texas — before the rules governing this new technology have even been finalized. Electric air taxis get the green light for test flights in Texas The flights will be conducted under the White House’s new pilot program to test out electric, hybrid, and autonomous aircraft. Earlier this year, the Federal Aviation Administration’s Advanced Air Mobility and Electric Vertical Takeoff and Landing (eVTOL) Integration Pilot Program (eIPP) selected eight state-led projects to serve as some of the first public tests of these new aircraft. The first one kicks off today in Texas, featuring three eVTOL companies: Joby, Beta, and Wisk. For the next week, these companies will conduct test flights demonstrating future routes between cities and regional airports, including Dallas Fort Worth International Airport. The aircraft won’t carry any passengers, but regulators will be keen to see how the state’s air traffic control system handles the uptick in flight traffic. The companies, meanwhile, are eager to prove to the federal government that their aircraft deserve to be awarded type certification, which is required before any of them can carry passengers commercially in the US. But type certification can take years to attain, which led to the White House to create this pilot program allowing these companies to demonstrate their new technology — even before the regulatory process has concluded. Through the eIPP, the companies hope to accelerate their path to market by getting a head start on data collection that will be needed for certification. Data from the program will also be used to “develop new regulations that safely enable this futuristic technology at scale,” the White House said earlier. The companies say they are thrilled to demonstrate the future of electric and autonomous flight, which they argue will help reduce car traffic in cities and open up new mobility opportunities for consumers. “I’m incredibly excited by the potential for vertical lift in Texas, a state with the infrastructure, expertise, and partnerships to help lead the next era of American aviation,” JoeBen Bevirt, Founder and CEO of Joby Aviation, said in a statement. Several of these companies have conducted public test flights before — Joby’s egg-shaped aircraft demonstrated its future route between Lower Manhattan and JFK Airprot earlier this year — but these will be the first official flights under the White House’s new pilot program. Additional tests are being planned in New York, Utah, Pennsylvania, Louisiana, Florida, North Carolina, and New Mexico. Legal in-fighting, however, could muddy the picture for electric aviation. Joby and one of its rivals, Archer, are currently suing each other for stolen trade secrets and corporate espionage. Technology limitations, including battery weight and sensor decisions, could also hamper the rollout.

item.title: The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.35
With the iPhone Duo, Apple has pulled off a familiar trick. It arrives into a mature Android foldable market with a handful of hardware features we’ve mostly already seen elsewhere, but paired with a level of software polish that makes a lot of them feel new again. It’s those software flourishes that have me excited to try the iPhone Duo when it launches next month, but I’m less convinced that its hardware will be anything special. The iPhone Duo’s hardware doesn’t look special, but its software might be Android foldables have done most of this before, but rarely looked so good doing it. If Apple had gotten there first, the Duo’s biggest surprise would have been its squat, wide, passport-inspired shape. But its slow-moving supply chain meant that Huawei, Samsung, and Xiaomi all managed to beat Apple to market with similarly sized rivals, so the unusual design already feels fairly familiar — helped by Samsung’s aggressive efforts to market its new design. More has been made of Apple’s efforts to eliminate the foldable display’s crease, which seem to have been largely successful. Apple attributes it to a 100-component hinge, custom adhesives that allow the display layers to “glide” over one another, and a matte finish that reduces glare and reflections to make the crease harder to spot. Trying the phone at Apple’s event yesterday, Verge editor-in-chief Nilay Patel said that you can’t really see the crease, but that “if you go looking for it, you can definitely feel one.” It sounds, and looks, impressive, but Apple is far from the first to do it. Samsung made great strides in eliminating the crease on its Z Fold 8 and Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to new titanium display layers. Before that, Oppo all but eliminated its Find N6 crease by using 3D printing to fill the minute gaps across the hinge. I’d have to see all those phones side by side to see which crease is subtlest, but even if Apple does win, it won’t be by much. None of the iPhone Duo’s other standout hardware features are true firsts either. Google beat it to an IP68 rating, now even surpassed by Honor’s IP69. Samsung, Oppo, and Honor have all offered stylus support before — though Samsung has since dropped it. Samsung also moved on from the under-display selfie camera, which has always been hamstrung by poor photo and video quality and a distractingly visible patch on the screen. In other ways, the hardware even feels behind the competition. The Duo is the thickest of this new wave of wide foldables, though at 5.2mm when open it’s still thinner than the iPhone Air. The weight is a more obvious issue: The 254g Duo is 26 percent heavier than the Z Fold 8 — a 53g difference — which is going to be pretty noticeable. You have to go back to 2022’s Z Fold 4 to find a Samsung foldable that’s heavier, TriFold excluded. There’s also no evidence that Apple has adopted silicon-carbon batteries yet, which have allowed Samsung, Motorola, and other Android manufacturers to fit bigger capacities into the smaller spaces of foldable phones. Apple says the phone should still deliver a full 24 hours of regular use, but Honor’s Magic V6 uses silicon-carbon to deliver two days of life. The rear cameras are pretty basic too, with a pair of 48-megapixel shooters and no telephoto. That’s almost an exact match for the cameras on the Z Fold 8, but Google, Motorola, Xiaomi and others are now providing capable triple cameras across their foldable lines, and the iPhone Duo already lags behind. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them None of this is to say that the Duo looks like a bad piece of hardware. Every foldable phone is a compromise, and Apple has picked a similar set of compromises to Samsung in order to get this phone out the door at $1,999. It looks as good as any Android foldable on paper, but it doesn’t look better than many of them. Where that might change is the software. Google has made an effort to make Android more flexible and adaptable to suit folding phones, while OEMs deliver custom solutions to push things further, but none have rewritten the rulebook quite like Apple. The version of iOS 27 running on the iPhone Duo isn’t the same as on other iPhones, but it doesn’t match the iPad either. The biggest change takes the dock from the bottom of the display and lays it out vertically along the right-hand side. The Dynamic Island is turned vertical and thrown in here too, while the status bar collapses into a small circular icon in the top-right corner. This big change is bolstered by clever little touches throughout, like a dynamic blur effect that shifts as you open the screen, creating a fluidity no Android foldable has so far matched. It’s a total transformation of the iOS layout that specifically has foldables in mind. The point of all that change is to ensure consistency between the outer and inner screens. Open the iPhone Duo on the homescreen and almost everything will stay in place, making the move between screens feel seamless. That effect won’t hold in full-screen apps of course, which will adapt to fill the space, but that right-hand UI rail will be fixed. Locking the whole phone interface to the right-hand edge doesn’t sound great for left-handed users though, who are likely to find the Duo unusually awkward to use unless Apple adds the option to flip everything to the other side. StandBy mode has also been retooled for the Duo. Prop the phone down half-open and it will enter StandBy, letting you use it as a digital photo frame, smart display, or just get quick access to a few key widgets, like the clock. Finally, the $2,000 alarm clock you’ve always dreamed of. Not everything is as ambitious. Multitasking looks limited so far, with the option to run two apps in split-screen, including two windows of the same app, and save pairs to reopen together. Android rivals offer similar, but support three split-screen apps at once, and often more sitting in flexible, resizeable floating windows. But Apple’s software power doesn’t only lie in its OS. It’s the only phone manufacturer with the influence to shift the app ecosystem at large, and with the Duo it hopes to push third-party developers to adopt its best foldable features. It already showed off Netflix, Slack, and Zoom apps with custom Duo support, in some cases adapting dynamically depending on how flexed the hinge is. Android foldable features are still rare, with most apps simply changing size to fit the varying screens. Even that has its limits — I found a few apps ran awkwardly on the Fold 8’s short outer display. Apple is likely to have an easier time ensuring developers optimize their apps to suit both of the Duo’s displays. Most apps do little else to take advantage of dual displays, multiple cameras, or semi-open states like a tented mode. A few video apps adapt their playback controls when foldables are half-open, but that’s about it so far. Of course, some of those app developers might take their iOS foldable features and eventually roll them out to Android too, so Apple’s advantage might not last forever. It’ll take more time with the Duo to see exactly how it stacks up against the latest models from the Android side of life. So far it doesn’t look like Apple has surpassed its rivals on the hardware side, but its total control of software may give it an edge regardless.

item.title: Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game
item.description:
Source: The Verge Score: 3.14
Marvel’s Wolverine captures just how angry its lead character is. The latest PS5 exclusive from Spider-Man developer Insomniac, Wolverine is a straightforward action game that is at its best when you’re (literally) slicing through enemies or thrust into a sequence pulled from a blockbuster movie, like climbing the fuselage of a plane as it careens toward land or racing a motorcycle across rain-slicked city streets. It’s the kind of game that can really get your heart rate rising, and keeping Logan mad is a key part of the strategy. In many ways, it’s a throwback to straightforward action titles of the past — and it’s a refreshing change of pace in a medium saturated with live-service and open-world games. Wolverine on the PS5 goes back to a simpler (and bloodier) style of action game The next few months are packed with new games, and PlayStation goes old-school to cut through the noise. Though it comes from Insomniac, Wolverine is very different from Spider-Man, which thrust the web-slinger into an open-world version of New York City. Instead, this is a much more linear experience that feels like a combination of two other PlayStation staples: God of War and Uncharted. Rather than follow Wolverine as a member of the X-Men, the story instead has him as an often reluctant member of Team X, a mercenary group with similar pro-mutant aims but a much more violent approach. Instead of heroes like Cyclops and Professor X, Wolvy is joined by more villain-adjacent characters like Sabretooth, Mystique, and Nathaniel Essex, before eventually connecting with Jean Grey. The story pulls Logan and his companions across the globe, but it starts out relatively simple, as they investigate a rash of mutant disappearances connected to a billionaire arms dealer. The most important thing about both Wolverine the character and Wolverine the game is fighting. This is a hairy little dude who loves to scrap, and his mutant powers — healing and sharp claws — make it so that he is very good at it, able to both take a huge amount of damage and dish it out. And the best part of the game is how Wolverine-specific the action is. The combat is fast and violent and forces you to be aggressive. Wolverine can leap huge distances to take out foes and use his claws to both repel attacks and slice at enemies, often with very gruesome results. (At the end of a battle he’s usually coated in blood.) An important part of this is Wolverine’s rage level, which increases the more you fight. As his rage grows, it allows you to do two things: go absolutely berserk and kill a rash of enemies with a single blow, and use your healing power as a sort of extra life in case your health depletes. It’s a clever system that means you can’t sit back and play it safe. Wolverine isn’t chill, and you can’t be either. That’s the God of War side of Wolverine. The Uncharted side comes in the form of all of the over-the-top set-pieces you’re thrown into. I’ll refrain from detailing some of the best ones for spoiler reasons, but I’ll say that, just like in Uncharted, these moments make it feel like you’re playing out a wild sequence from an action movie. There are chases across the rooftops of Tokyo, massive boss battles against some iconic comic book villains, and scenes where Wolverine is literally being ripped apart as he fights for survival. The flip side is that, because of this setup, Wolverine is also much more restrictive than most of its contemporaries. In some ways this is a good thing; it’s refreshing to play a game that isn’t trying to do everything. But there are still some awkward elements. For instance, much like in Spider-Man, there are lots of collectibles that will reveal new bits of story or unlock new suits for Wolverine to wear. But exploration outside of the main path is extremely dull, so the only reason to track these down is if you have a completionist mindset. It’s also disappointing that Wolverine’s closet of outfits is much less fun than Spider-Man’s, and they often feel out of place with the game’s attempt at a more gritty tone. Making matters worse is that, despite a promising start, the story ends up in a largely forgettable place, with few surprises, particularly if you have an even slight knowledge of the X-Men universe from comics or the animated series. Outside of combat and set-pieces, Wolverine skews generic AAA game; the voice acting, the cutscenes, and even some of the missions feel like standard video game fare, many of which seem out of place. Wolverine is amazing when you’re surrounded by ninjas trying to kill you. But when Logan is in a tux trying to spy on a fancy party? Not so much. All that said, Wolverine’s return to a simpler and smaller style of action — I beat the game in around 13 hours — is still notable, particularly from Sony, which has had a rough few years after placing many ill-fated bets in the live-service space. But much like last year’s Ghost of Yōtei, Wolverine shows that PlayStation is still capable of the single-player blockbusters the platform is best known for. It’s also launching at perhaps the busiest video game release period in recent memory, going up against major titles including Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Control Resonant, Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave, Gears of War: E-Day, Silent Hill: Townfall, Star Wars: Zero Company, and, soon enough, The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Grand Theft Auto VI. In that company, despite occasionally skewing generic, Wolverine’s bloodthirsty focus on action is something that makes it stand out. Marvel’s Wolverine launches on September 15th on the PS5.

item.title: After a Mat, These Cork Blocks Are the Yoga Props Worth Investing In
item.description:
Source: Wirecutter Score: 3.27
If you’ve ever attended a class at a yoga studio, you’ve probably seen yoga blocks. These rectangular props are intended to provide additional support and reach, making some poses more accessible to people with varying skill levels and physical abilities. Experts say that after a reliable mat, yoga blocks (ideally two, so you have one for each arm or leg or to stack, if desired) are the equipment most likely to elevate your practice. If you want to invest in a set for use at home, we’ve determined that the Manduka Cork Yoga Block is the one to get. Everything we recommend What to consider - Cork or foamYoga blocks made of cork tend to be heavier, stiffer, and especially supportive. Foam blocks are lighter, softer, and less stable. - Size and weightMost yoga blocks are around 9 by 6 by 4 inches. Foam blocks are usually lighter than cork ones. - Your practiceCork blocks are better for balancing and standing. Foam blocks are preferred for restorative poses. - Two > oneGenerally, two blocks will serve your practice best. Some poses require only one. Top pick This block’s edges are nicely rounded, and its sides have an extra-grippy texture, reducing slippage. It’s on the heavier side, however. With its rounded edges and a satisfyingly grippy texture, the sturdy but comfortable Manduka Cork Yoga Block is exceptionally versatile, supporting bodies in all manner of standing/balancing and restorative poses. At about 2 pounds, it’s among the heaviest cork blocks available, lending additional stability but adding heft. Runner-up Although this block is lighter than our pick, it stably supports bodies in balancing poses. Its texture also provides good grip. The JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block is a lighter alternative to our pick, so it’s easier to move around during practice (or to travel with). It’s also narrower, which may appeal to those with smaller hands. Because its edges aren’t as rounded as those of our pick, this block is somewhat less comfortable to use in reclined positions, such as under the sacrum in a bridge pose. Why you should trust us To learn all we could about yoga blocks, we spoke with yoga instructors, yoga therapists, and block manufacturers. - I’m a longtime yoga enthusiast, and in 2023, I completed 200-hour yoga teacher training with Three Sisters Yoga. It was during this training that I embraced using yoga blocks. I’ve also contributed reporting to our yoga mats guide and reviewed hot yoga towels. - Like all Wirecutter journalists, I review and test products with complete editorial independence. I’m never made aware of any business implications of our editorial recommendations. Read more about our editorial standards. Who this is for Contrary to popular belief, blocks aren’t just for beginners. They’re for anyone and everyone who practices yoga, and they can be especially useful to people with physical limitations or injuries. Using blocks is not a sign of being “bad” at yoga. Blocks are useful for balancing, standing, stretching, and restorative yoga poses, among other things. The experts we consulted explained that blocks can serve various purposes beyond providing additional reach and support, making them arguably the most versatile yoga props. They aid in deepening stretches, bringing the ground closer, and getting into proper alignment without compromising your body (especially the spine, knees, and hips). You can even use them for core-strengthening exercises. Yoga therapist and author Jenny Clise emphasized that you can use a block for assistance in getting into a challenging pose. The block serves to reduce fear or to form muscle memory. The use of blocks involves “curiosity and investigation,” Clise said. How we picked and tested Yoga blocks can be made of wood, bamboo, cork, or foam. Blocks made of maple or bamboo are gorgeous, but they’re not the most economical or practical (slippage is common). For this guide, we focused on blocks made of cork and foam, two comparatively less expensive materials that provide better grip. Altogether, we tried nine top-rated best-sellers. In choosing what to test, we considered: - Weight: A good cork block should be sturdy and stable in standing/balancing poses. If it’s too heavy, however, it won’t be comfortable to move around during your practice or to carry outside the home. Foam blocks, usually made of EVA foam, will be lighter but should still be stable enough to hold some weight. The cork and foam blocks we tested ranged from 0.4 pounds to 2.4 pounds each. - Size: The standard block (whether cork or foam) is roughly 9 by 6 by 4 inches. All of the blocks we tested were about this size. - Material quality/texture: The cork should provide good grip and a comfortable surface. There should be little to no cork shavings that rub off during practice — at least in the beginning, before heavy use. Foam will naturally have a little more cushion, so we preferred high-density foam blocks that felt soft but were still durable. - Edge design: Some blocks are well rounded; others have a more pointed edge. Rounded edges add extra comfort. I used a set of two blocks for each practice because many poses require two blocks for balance. I did the same poses with each of the block sets, including downward dog, triangle, half moon, reclining bound angle, and bridge pose. We also sought feedback from people who have used our picks longer term — in some cases, for years. We’ll continue to long-term test our picks and report back on their longevity. Our pick: Manduka Cork Yoga Block Top pick This block’s edges are nicely rounded, and its sides have an extra-grippy texture, reducing slippage. It’s on the heavier side, however. Sturdy and long-lasting, the Manduka Cork Yoga Block has the grippiest texture and the most comfortable edges of all the blocks we tested. It’s ideal to use for standing and balancing poses, but it can also be used for restorative ones. Cork is long-lasting and has natural cushion that’s not too soft. Cork blocks tend to last a long time, even if shavings inevitably rub off over the years. Krissy Jones, cofounder of Sky Ting Yoga in New York, said she’s been practicing at home with her Manduka cork blocks for about eight years. “They seem totally fine. I don’t think I need to replace them anytime soon.” The block’s sides and ends are grippier than those of other, similar blocks. So there will be less slipping while balancing or being supported in stretches. The texture of the cork on the sides of this block is somewhat rough but still plenty comfortable against the skin. The faces of this block have a slightly smoother surface, which you can use while in downward dog. According to Deanna Green, owner of Shambhala Yoga & Dance Center in Brooklyn, New York, cork blocks are better than foam for downward dog or plank. If your hands don’t have a little warmth to them, you may feel the slightest slip in downward dog while using two of these blocks. As your hands progressively develop a little more moisture, the blocks work better to keep you from slipping. This added height from the blocks may be beneficial for those who have a hard time holding downward dog or want to practice at an elevated height. This 2-pound block remains stable while balancing. It didn’t budge while I balanced, and I had no issue using it for incorporated core exercises. In fact, that extra weight feels like you’re getting a more vigorous workout. Its rounded edges are very comfortable. They felt better than those of any other cork block we tested. Along with the thickness, the rounded edges make the blocks comfortable to grab or lean on — even in reclining hero pose. Dimensions: 8.75 by 5.75 by 3.88 inches Weight: 2.16 pounds Material: cork Flaws but not dealbreakers The Manduka cork blocks are among the heaviest we considered — yet they are still easy to move around during practice. They also may feel a bit too wide for people who have smaller hands. Runner-up: JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block Runner-up Although this block is lighter than our pick, it stably supports bodies in balancing poses. Its texture also provides good grip. The JadeYoga Large Cork Yoga Block is a solid block that performs almost as well as our pick and generally costs a bit less. Its edges are rounded, but not as prominently as those of the Manduka cork block. The cork has a good grip. We found that this block did not slip when we used it. However, unlike those of the Manduka cork block, the faces and sides of the JadeYoga block don’t feel any different, so this block is slightly less satisfying to use. The faces are not as smooth as those of our main pick, and the sides aren’t as grippy. The weight feels just right. At 1.74 pounds, the JadeYoga block has the most comfortable weight of all the blocks we tested. It’s lighter than our pick but remains stable throughout practice. This block is a tad slimmer than our pick. So people with smaller hands may prefer it over the Manduka cork block. Dimensions: 8.75 by 5.75 by 3.75 inches Weight: 1.74 pounds Material: cork Another yoga block worth considering If you want a lighter, softer block that’s ideal for restorative yoga: The Calia Foam Yoga Block is lighter than our cork picks (just 0.8 pounds), yet it’s surprisingly stable, including for standing poses. Compared with the firmer, heavier cork blocks we recommend, this foam block is a better choice for restorative poses. The Calia block, made of EVA foam, is comfortable to sit on and to use in reclining positions. Its surface and edges are pleasantly smooth and soft, but still plenty firm and supportive. The blocks we tested had visibly uneven texture — like all foam blocks it is subject to indentation and scratches. And while EVA foam can be recycled, it’s not particularly easy to. The competition The Alo Uplifting Yoga Block feels rough and is quite hard for a foam block. The Bala Building Block’s edges are not as comfortable as those on other foam blocks we tested, and its overall width makes this block more difficult to grasp. At about 2 pounds, the Calia Cork Yoga Block is stable and hefty. The edges of this block are rounded, but overall it’s neither as smooth nor as grippy as our picks. Gaiam’s Cork Yoga Block is exceptionally sturdy (and the thickest block we tested). But it’s 2.4 pounds, which we found was too heavy for comfort. Hugger Mugger’s Cork Yoga Block has a nice, grippy texture, but it’s a little too slim, and it wobbles more easily than our picks. The Hugger Mugger 4-Inch Foam Yoga Block’s beveled edges can feel a little sharp in reclined poses. Note that the marble-patterned version of this block was far too light to feel stable, and it weighs around half what the solid-color version does (they were supposed to weigh the same, according to the company’s marketing). We chose not to test both the Lululemon’s Lift and Lengthen Yoga Block and Inner Flow Yoga Block Marble. The former is thinner and lighter than the Manduka Recycled Foam Yoga Block we previously recommended, making it less versatile and potentially less stable. The extra rounded edge is less suitable for restorative practices; this block would likely be best for balancing poses. Some cork from the Yoga Accessories 4” Cork Yoga Block rubbed off on our mat during practice. Yoga Hustle’s The Block, made of EVA foam, comes in fun patterns. It performed nearly the same as the Calia Foam Block we recommend, with similar weight and dimensions. At the time of publication it was out of stock.
